en: *Laghutantraṭīkā*, Chapter I: The Foundation of Tantra **Introduction** Oṃ! Homage to the glorious Cakrasaṃvara! Having bowed to Him—who, with His left and right feet, has trampled upon Śiva and the daughter of the Snowy Mountain (Pārvatī) as they stand upon the sun; who has terrified the gods, the lords of spirits and asuras, along with the hosts of planets, by His wrathful gaze; and who wears the insignia of the elephant hide, tiger skin, serpent, skull-cup, and garland of heads—I shall write this commentary on that very Tantra, which seeks out the clear vajra-words.
[1] Urged by Vīreśa, this was composed by me, Śrīvajrapāṇi,
for the sake of the yogins’ acquisition of merit and for the attainment of the fruit of Mahāmudrā.
[2] Now, therefore, the essence extracted from the *Lakṣābhidhāna* Tantra is the Śrī Heruka Mahāyoga, the Saṃvara of the Circle of Ḍākinīs.
[3] In this time of the five degenerations, for the sake of attaining the fruits of merit and wisdom,
the Vajrī, requested by Vārāhī, shall reveal the *Laghutantra*.
[4] For the benefit of practitioners who have short lifespans and little vigor,
and who are possessed of passion, hatred, and so forth, it was taught by means of that very method.
[5] Abiding eternally within the secret, the secret of the ḍākinīs, and the self of all;
consisting of all female messengers, the being Vajrasattva is great bliss.
[6] This Blessed One is the Self-Existent, the accomplisher of all desires and aims;
she has emerged in the form of Sound, whose sphere of activity is the conduct of the *samaya*.
[7] Difficult to find in the three worlds, abiding in the beginning, middle, and end,
is the sequence of the ritual procedure for mantra-yoga, produced from the churning-stick and the act of churning.
[8] That very thing by which the denotable is expressed is called the denotation;
it is Heruka, innate bliss, the supreme middle breath.
[9] Endowed with feces, urine, the moon, and the sun, along with the four channels—
Kulikā, Vajravārāhī, and Mahāmudrā, who is without support— the yogin, having abandoned the bliss of the action-seal (karmamudrā), should worship her by means of that.
[10 1/2] Thus, this meaning of the consecration, which was not revealed due to the brevity of the tantra and was stated merely by way of summary, is here expanded upon by means of this commentary.

Regarding the subject matter and contents of this tantra: first, having thoroughly considered the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the expression (*abhidhāna*), the relationship (*sambandha*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the ultimate purpose of the purpose (*prayojanaprayojana*), the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka—who resides in the supreme secret, is surrounded by heroes and heroines, and was requested by Vajravārāhī—taught this tantra, which bestows the state of Buddhahood in this very life through the intention of one's own mind for those disciples who are free from conventional restraints.
It is the most essential of essences extracted from the *Mūlatantra* known as the *Lakṣābhidhāna*, and it consists of seven hundred verses.
Here, the Blessed Lord Heruka, whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means, is the subject matter (*abhidheya*). The King of Tantras, which elucidates him, is the expression (*abhidhāna*).
Between these two—the subject matter and the expression—there exists a relationship characterized by that of the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācaka-lakṣaṇa*).

The purpose is the accomplishment of worldly siddhis through means such as entering the mandala for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. The ultimate purpose is Buddhahood, which is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā-siddhi by means of the accumulations of merit and wisdom.
Having clearly perceived these [purposes].
"Of those people to be trained who are devoid of restraint"—here, "restraint" refers to the vows of a Śrāvaka monk; those who lack such restraint are "devoid of restraint.
Their own mental disposition consists of passion, hatred, and so forth.

By that very intention of his own mind, even in this life, [he attains] the bestower of Buddhahood. By that same means of cultivation (*bhāvanopāya*), for practitioners in this age of the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*) who possess short lifespans and little vigor,
it is "by abiding in the supreme secret."

The secret is the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), which is the element of space; [he is] situated there, abiding in the supreme secret, surrounded by heroes and heroines. The "heroes" are the twenty-four [deities] such as Khaṇḍakapālin and others, who move like the moon.
The Heroines, such as Ḍākinī and the others, are the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) by nature.
He is surrounded by them; thus, he is "surrounded by Heroes and Heroines.
Being requested by Vajravārāhī, the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka said: "From the syllable *Śrī* comes non-dual gnosis; from the syllable *He* comes that which is free from causes."
From the letter *ru* it is liberated from form; from the letter *ka* it is devoid of instruments of action.
"Bhaga" refers to one endowed with qualities such as sovereignty; or, because he shatters Māra, he is "bhaga. He who possesses that is called the Bhagavān, the Lord of the three realms.
Thus, by that Blessed Śrī Heruka, from the *Mūlatantra* known as the *Lakṣābhidhāna*, this essence— a tantra measuring one hundred thousand verses— was taught.
And that Blessed One abides by way of the nature of other tantras;
first, he abides by way of the nature of the place of dwelling,
and thereafter, he abides by way of the nature of the conduct of the pledge (*samaya*).
Then he abides in the nature of the requester and the instructor; he abides in the nature of the worship of the *kulikā*;
then he abides in the nature of the worship for the attainment of the female messengers (*dūtī*).
He abides in the nature of the cultivation for the accomplishment of desire.
Thereafter, he abides in the nature of making offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others by means of the drops of bodhicitta.
He abides in the nature of liberation from all sins.
Then he abides by way of having the nature of accomplishing the state of a yogin; he abides by way of having the nature of observing the commitments (samaya);
then he abides by way of having the nature of guarding against the violation of the commitments.
He abides in the nature of consuming the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).

Then, in the *gaṇacakra*, with the thumb and ring finger, he abides in the nature of tasting the drinking of the moon (*soma*) in the mouth; he abides in the nature of the union of the two organs (*dvīndriyasamāpatti*).
Then, he abides in the nature of praising divine bliss. Thus it is said: "Divine and human happiness is not worth even a sixteenth part (*kalā*) of the imperishable divine bliss."
Thus, in the first section on the meaning of the alms-food, the Blessed One is established.
(3) Then, he abides by way of having the nature of fixed locations such as mountain caves;
he abides by way of having the nature of the ten principles (*tattva*) beginning with the mandala;
and then, he abides by way of having the nature of the worship of the mandala-circle of the Guru, the Vīras, and the Vīreśvarīs.
He abides in the nature of the initiation of the disciple into the maṇḍala;
then he abides in the nature of the bestowing of empowerment;
and he abides in the nature of the worship of the mudrā and the preceptor.
Thus the Blessed One remained in the section on the mandala consecration.
Then he abides as the nature of the manifestation of the realm of the ḍākinīs; he abides as the nature of the extraction of mantras;
then he abides as the nature of the extensive activity of the King of Vidyās.
He abides as having the nature of accomplishing the eight mundane siddhis;
from that, he abides as having the nature of performing the secret gestures (choma);
and he abides as having the nature characterized by the action-seal (karmamudrā).
Then he abides by way of the inherent nature of their conversation and the acts of coming and going;
he abides by way of the inherent nature of the characteristics of the ḍākinīs;
and then he abides by way of the inherent nature of beholding the mudrās and counter-mudrās.
He abides by way of having the nature of not speaking of the name of the *samaya*.
He abides by way of having the nature of the eight great worldly and transcendent *samayas*.
Thereafter, he abides by way of having the nature of eating a single *caruka* offering.
He abides as the intrinsic nature of the offering of the sacrificial oblation (*balidāna*).

Thereafter, he abides as the intrinsic nature of the extraction of the mantra of Sumbharāja. He abides as the intrinsic nature of the accomplishment of the expansion of his activities (*karmaprasara*).
He abides by way of having the nature of meditating on the mantra-image;
then he abides by way of having the nature of cultivating the non-conceptual reality; then he abides by way of having the nature of supramundane fire-offering (*homa*).

Then, he abides by way of having the nature of reciting the mantras of the Vajra-Mind and so forth, situated between the names of the Hero and the Mistress of Heroes accompanied by the mantra-syllables of the four faces and the rest.
He abides as the nature of the instruction on the ten stages, beginning with the *piṭha*, and the twenty-four locations;
he abides as the nature of the placement of the head and so forth;
he abides as the nature of the purity of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.
Then, he abides as the nature of the purification of the twenty-four elements, beginning with Khaṇḍakapāla;
he abides as the nature of the transformation of the forms of the goddesses, the Bhūcaras, and the Khēcaras;
and he abides as the nature of the authority over enjoyment and dissolution through the movement of the wheel of worship by the women of the thirty-seven families.
He abides by virtue of having the nature of turning the wheel of Dharma;
he abides by virtue of having the nature of the Nirmāṇakāya, Saṃbhogakāya, and Dharmakāya; and he abides by virtue of having a nature in which emptiness and compassion are inseparable.
Thus, the Blessed One Śrī Heruka abides as the very nature of the tantra.
The opening of the tantra reveals itself as the subject matter through this very title, by means of such passages as:
"Now, therefore, I shall speak of the secret in brief, and not at length.
One might object: "In every king of tantras, there is an indication of the place where [the teaching] was given, beginning with 'Thus have I heard' and so forth."
How is it that in this tantra, by means of the passage beginning with "Then, therefore, the secret," the Blessed One has indicated the location where he dwelt?
In the *Samāja*, *Hevajra*, and other Yoga and Yoginī tantras, the word of the Blessed One is considered true because they begin with "Thus have I heard.
Therefore, this tantra was not taught by the Blessed One.
Thus, there may be the opinion of some who seek refuge in the literal expression (*vyañjana*).
Therefore, it is said:

here, that which must be stated for future generations by those foolish people who rely solely on the literal expression—that the King of Tantras was spoken by the Blessed One without [the introductory formula] "Thus have I heard" and so forth—does not exist.
That is not so.
Why?
Because here, the Blessed One has elsewhere taught the four reliances.
That is to say:
relying on the meaning, not relying on the letter;
relying on knowledge, not relying on consciousness.
Relying on the definitive meaning, not on the interpretable meaning;
relying on the Dharma, not on the person.
Therefore, according to these words of the Blessed One, reliance on the literal expression was never taught by the Blessed One in any vehicle.
The collection of vowels and consonants is a mere designation that expresses the existence or non-existence of the phenomena of those who possess designations.
In this world, many designations can occur for even a single phenomenon of existence or non-existence;
yet among them, no single designation will be either primary or secondary.
Because all [these terms] establish the property of being both existent and non-existent as one;

for instance, terms such as "woman," "lady," and "young woman" establish the property of existence characterized by having breasts and hair, while terms such as "sky-flower," "space-nature," and "hare's horn" establish the property of non-existence.
In this way, in all cases, the relationship between the designation (*saṃjñā*) and the designated (*saṃjñin*) is to be understood by yogins.
Here, the letter *a*, which indicates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), becomes the letter *e* when ending in the locative case.
Therefore, by the designation *ata e*, the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is understood as the support of all.

Thus, the Blessed One said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*: "In space, which is non-inert, clear, and luminous where there is no room [for obstruction], in the universal vajra-abode, the place of dissolution, the delightful element of all."
By such [statements] as this:
"He is eternally established in the supreme, delightful secret, which is the self of all."
Thus, up to this point, various designations for the term "dwelt" (*vijahāra*) have been stated by way of specific qualifiers. Likewise, in the *Śrī-samāja* and other tantras:
"Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One dwelt within the wombs (*bhaga*) of the vajra women who are the heart of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas."
This [reality] also has many names:
it is considered to be the Bhaga, the Lotus, the Pure, the Abode of Bliss,
Sukhāvatī, the Lion Throne, the Supportless, Suchness (tathatā), and the Perfection (pāramitā).
Thus is the support; likewise, that which is supported:
"Vaṃ, the wielder of the vajra, the bestower of boons, the speaker, the innate bliss, the imperishable."
Śiva is peaceful, auspicious, the Lord, omnipresent, and supreme.
Thus, by means of these and many other designations,
the Knowledge Body (jñānakāya), which is without parts, is proclaimed by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "It is to be established [as such]."
The support is the Perfection of Wisdom, which is of all aspects yet non-conceptual;
that which is to be supported is revealed as compassion that is without objective referent.
Thus, it is said in another tantra: "That which is divine, shaped like the letter E, adorned in the center with the syllable Vaṃ, is the abode of all blisses, a jewel-casket for the Buddhas."
Thus it is said:
"Without beginning or end, peaceful, the destruction of existence and non-existence, all-pervading."
The indivisibility of emptiness and compassion is known as bodhicitta.

(6) Thus, in many various tantras, this yoga consisting of wisdom and means has been taught by the Blessed One. Therefore, Buddhists should not say that a tantra is taught by the Blessed One only where it begins with "Thus have I [heard]" (*evam mayā*) and so forth.
Where there is no [fault], that does not occur.
Here, in the Mantra system, because one grasps at faults regarding phenomena not seen, a root downfall occurs.
Due to a root downfall, those who are conceited about what they have falsely heard go to the Avīci hell.

Thus, for this reason, the teaching of the tantra beginning with "Now, therefore, the secret" (*athāto rahasyam*) and so forth is not contradictory in this tantra, because it establishes the dharma consisting of wisdom and skillful means whose nature is emptiness and compassion.
Regarding this, it is said in the *Lakṣābhidhāna*: "In that tantra wherein the unity of emptiness and compassion is revealed..."
The means of accomplishment of the Lord of the World—that tantra was taught by the Buddha.
Regarding the accomplishment of worldly siddhis by means of conventional truth (lokasaṃvṛtisatya),
the cultivation of conceptual thought is taught, as well as the procedure for mantra recitation.
From the perspective of ultimate truth, the Tathāgatas have taught that meditation, which is free from all conceptual constructions,
is for the sake of accomplishing the Gnosis Body (jñānakāya).
Thus ends the rule for the consecration of the tantra.

(7) Chapter II: Surface Meaning and Deep Meaning. Commentary on CS 1: Now, the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) as taught in the Tantra are being expounded, beginning with the words "Next, therefore, I shall speak of the secret.

Next, immediately after the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Vajrabhairava, the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka—having entered the meditative absorption of the *Ḍākinīcakrasaṃvara*—addressed Vajravārāhī, based upon the *Lakṣābhidhāna*.

"O Vajravārāhī, listen! I shall explain to you in brief, and not at length, that very secret known as Heruka which is proclaimed in the *Lakṣābhidhāna-tantra* as the yoga and the knowledge of the ritual procedure taught in the tantra.
For what reason, O Blessed One, do you teach this minor tantra from the Root Tantra?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this age of the five degenerations, the humans of Jambudvīpa—especially those in the Noble Land—will have short lifespans and little wisdom.
Those who are Vajrācāryas will fall into root downfalls."
The monks will become practitioners of the ten unwholesome actions; householders will become consumers of the property of the Three Jewels;
and the learned will become commentators on tantras they have not heard.
Out of pride in their own scholarship, they will become authors of commentaries and sub-commentaries on the tantras;
by teaching the meaning of the tantras erroneously, they will go to hell.
Those foolish Buddhists, due to their dull-witted faith, will perform services for householders who act as teachers.
They will revile those who uphold the banner of the Omniscient One. Those who are disciples will become seekers of faults in their true gurus.
They will offer praise and worship to false gurus who are like devouring demons.
They will not practice the word of the Buddha as taught for the propitiation of the Guru.
(8) Those who teach the Dharma will become promoters of the ten unwholesome actions.
Practitioners will become attached to speech, food, drink, and sensual enjoyments.
Women will become excessively greedy for sensual pleasures;
therefore, the Buddha taught this abbreviated tantra from among all the root tantras.

And that [abbreviated teaching] is to be understood by wise seekers of liberation through the instruction of a true guru—given according to other tantras—and through commentaries composed by Bodhisattvas, because it abounds in vajra-words.
Therefore, I shall speak of the secret in brief rather than in detail.
Regarding the term "secret": according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), it refers to the *karmamudrā* and the *bhaga*;
according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), it refers to the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the union with Śrī Heruka.
*Śrī* means innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
*He* means it is devoid of the causes of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*).
*Ru* means form (*rūpa*) is free from defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
"Ka" refers to that which is devoid of the instruments such as the eyes and so forth, characterized by non-referential compassion.
Its union with emptiness—that is, its oneness—is the inseparability of emptiness and compassion; this I shall explain.

According to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), Śrī Heruka is the male organ; its union with the female vulva is their oneness. I shall explain this for the sake of the accumulation of merit for those foolish people who desire the pleasure of the two organs, for the sake of liberating the mind from other objects, and as a means to accomplish all desired aims—this is the qualification of the ritual action (*karmapada*).
"I shall speak"—thus it should be understood that the *ātmanepada* ending is used everywhere in the sense of the agent.

Here, in the external sense according to the *neyārtha*, the goal of all desires—the sovereignty of mundane qualities such as *aṇimā* and so forth—arises through the yoga of the mantra, karma, jñāna, and mudrā.
Its means of accomplishment is the aforementioned "knowledge of wisdom" (*prajñājñāna*).

In the definitive sense (*nītārtha*), "Vajrasattva" refers to the Perfectly Awakened One who fulfills all desires; his purpose is the turning of the wheel of Dharma, characterized by omniscience, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth.
That which accomplishes this is the "accomplisher of the purpose of all desires.
Thus, I shall explain the yoga that is inseparable from emptiness and compassion.

(9) "And even higher than the high. Here, "the high" refers to the happiness of the objects of human desire; higher than that is the happiness of those who have attained their desires in the realms of the *rūpa* and *arūpa* worlds, which is endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya*) and so forth.

Even higher than that high [happiness], in the state of perfect realization, is the supreme high—the happiness of the Omniscient One, endowed with all qualities of sovereignty, the teacher of all phenomena, possessing all aspects, and all-pervading.
"Even higher than the high" refers to the *Ḍākinīcakrasaṃvara*.
Here, according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), "ḍākinīs" refers to Vajraḍākinī and the others.
Within the self, thirty-six channels are situated in the wheels of gnosis, mind, speech, and body, as well as in the eight gates beginning with the mouth.
These very [channels] are designated by the names of the *ātmapīṭha* and so forth, ending with the *ucchiṣṭa* and the cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*).

Externally, in the eight directions of Meru, according to the sequence to be described, the indication of the locations such as the countries and the head is to be understood as the support (*ādhāra*) for those possessing the quality of being supported (*ādheya*).
The *cakra* of these *ḍākinīs* is their assembly (*samūha*).

Its *saṃvara*—meaning its unification or gathering (*ekatva*, *melāpaka*)—together with Heruka, within one’s own sacred seats (*ātmapīṭha*) and so forth, is the "Gathering of the Circle of *ḍākinīs*" (*ḍākinīcakrasaṃvara*).
Heruka, too, is accompanied by the Heroines (*savīra*) and consists of twenty-five aspects.
Vajravārāhī, together with the Vīreśvarīs, consists of thirty-seven aspects.
The *saṃvara*—the gathering (*melāpaka*)—of these ḍākinīs is with Heruka and the twenty-four heroes.
Herein, the *saṃvara* of the twelve messengers (*dūtī*) is with Heruka.

The *saṃvara* of the twenty-four female messengers together with the heroes is expressed by means of the seed-syllables of the mantra through the union of the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*). In this regard, there are thirty-six *yoginī* tantras; each one, beginning with the letter *ka*, consists of thirty-six deities of the maṇḍala, accompanied by the collection of vowels.
Without a leader, there are no two leaders consisting of the thirty-seven [bodhipākṣika-dharmas].
Herein, first, the *Kavajra-tantra* is described:
at the pericarp of the womb-gnosis-wheel (*garbhajñānacakra*), there is the syllable *HŪṂ*, which consists of the five voids (*pañcaśūnya*).

In the cardinal petals: *a ā aṃ aḥ*. In the intermediate petals: *ka kā kaṃ kaḥ*. By way of the division of the qualities (*guṇabheda*), in the cardinal directions of the cremation grounds: *ka kā kaṃ kaḥ*; in the corners: *ka kā kaṃ kaḥ*.
In the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*), there are *ki*, *kṛ*, *ku*, and *kḷ* in the cardinal directions, and *kī*, *kṛī*, *kū*, and *kḹ* in the intermediate directions.
In the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*), there are the *guṇa* [and *vṛddhi*] vowels.
By differentiation, in the cardinal directions there are *ke*, *kar*, *ko*, and *kal*; in the intermediate directions, *kai*, *kār*, *kau*, and *kāḷ*.

In the body wheel (*kāyacakre*), through the substitution of *yaṇ*, in the cardinal directions there are *kya*, *kra*, *kva*, and *kla*; in the intermediate directions, *kyā*, *krā*, *kvā*, and *klā*.
Thus, the consonants produced by the qualities of wind, fire, water, and earth become twenty-four-fold within the three wheels.
That which is raised by means of the nature of the void-syllables becomes twelvefold together with that which is raised in the wheel of gnosis within the eight cremation grounds.
By that, there is the *saṃvara* [union] of those ḍākinīs who possess the nature of the void-syllables, together with the one whose form is non-referential compassion.
[This refers to] the Blessed One, who possesses twelve eyes.
"Vajra" refers to union with Vārāhī; likewise, "union" refers to the twenty-four Heroines being in union with the twenty-four Heroes.
According to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), this is the *Cakrasaṃvara* of the *Ḍākinī*-wheel.
In this way, there are the [mantras] beginning with Kha-kāra-vajra and so forth;
namely: ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma; ta, tha, da, dha, na; sa, pa, ṣa, śa, ka; la, va, ra, ya; ha, kṣa.
These are the thirty-six leaders of the Yoginī Tantras.
The leaders of the Yoga Tantras as well:
those maṇḍala deities produced from a single seed-syllable belong to one [tantra],
while those maṇḍala deities generated from thirty-six distinct seed-syllables belong to different tantras and families.
"They are not to be understood as a single family; rather, they are the three families, the five families, the single nature, and the hundred families," according to the word of the Blessed One.
"The yogi must understand the tantra, which consists of various families, by relying on the reliance upon the meaning"—this is the rule of the Tathāgata.
Thus, according to worldly convention, the *Cakrasaṃvara* of the *Ḍākinī*-circle is for the sake of accomplishing mundane siddhis.
In its definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), it is called the *Cakrasaṃvara* of the *ḍākinīs*.
"Ḍākinīs" refers to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*).
Their "circle" (*cakra*) is their assembly, characterized as the *dharmakāya* and having emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its essence.
His union (*saṃvara*) with the *svābhāvikakāya*, which consists of non-referential compassion, is oneness.
Here, compassion is the moon—the unobscured great bliss characterized by the twenty-five lunar digits, which is the bodhicitta.
The sun consists of the twelve emptinesses.
The *saṃvara* together with that [is] the *Ḍākinīcakrasaṃvara*; "I shall explain that"—this is the rule of action (*kriyāniyama*).
In the manner thus described:
(11) "Abiding always within the secret, supreme, and delightful self of all, the being (*sattva*) consisting of all female messengers (*dūtī*), Vajrasattva, is supreme bliss."
Thus:

here, in the previously mentioned sphere of emptiness (*śūnyadhātu*), which possesses the nature of all things, one is always—throughout all time, past, future, and present—established because of the absence of the phenomena of arising and destruction;
[therefore] the being (*sattva*) consists of all female messengers (*dūtī*).

The female messengers (*dūtī*) are *ḍākinīs*; they are equal to space, having abandoned the obscurations of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), and they move through space.
This is because the root list (*dhātupāṭha*) states that the root *ḍai* means "to go through the air.
They do not harm all sentient beings; they are village deities who reside in sacred seats (*pīṭha*), secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), and so forth.

These are pure by nature as the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). A sentient being consisting of those [factors] consists of all the female messengers (*dūtī*); he is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) characterized by the three realms.
Vajrasattva is supreme bliss.
The fourth is the *sahajakāya*, meaning supreme bliss, which is immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*).
The unity of these two—the *dharmakāya* and the *sahajakāya*—is called Vajrasattva.
"Vajra" refers to the *dharmakāya*, emptiness, and wisdom (*prajñā*).
"Sattva" is the sahajakāya; compassion is the means (upāya).
Thus, the union of Heruka, consisting of wisdom and means, is designated as Vajrasattva.
Commentary on CS 3CD: "This Blessed One, the Self-Arisen, is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*."
In this context, Svayambhū is Brahmā; and since it is stated in another tantra that "Vairocana is Kāyavajra, and Brahmā is the Holder of Kāyavajra," he is to be understood through that other tantra.
And it is as follows:
in the *Māyājāla*, the Blessed One said: "Svayambhū arises from space; he is the great fire of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*)."
Vairocana is the great radiance; Virocana is the light of gnosis.

This should be understood through the verses beginning with "ītyādinā" and ending with "vajrāṅkuśo mahāpāśaḥ. The self-arisen Vairocana is the *nirmāṇakāya*, endowed with the excellence of all aspects; such is the rule of the *Ḍākinījālasamvara*.
[Commentary on CS 4AB: Having emerged in the form of sound, she is the sphere of the conduct of the *samaya*.

Thus, because of the single union with the *sahaja-dharma-nirmāṇakāya*, the *saṃbhogakāya* consists of sound and is characterized by the unstruck resonance (*anāhata-dhvani*) of all-encompassing gnosis.
The form of the mantra, whose nature is that [of the *saṃbhogakāya*], is the object of the conventional practices; the deity of the mantra, whose form is sound, is the unstruck speech.
This conventional practice (*samayācāra*) is to be explained in what follows, by means of which she becomes accessible as an object of experience (*gocara*).
And thus the Blessed One said: "The great-sounding bell of Dharma, the great drum of Dharma, the drum of the Dharma in the ten directions, he who is the non-abiding nirvāṇa."
Thus [ends the commentary].
Commentary on CS 4cd: That which abides in the beginning, middle, and end is difficult to find within the three worlds.
Thus: this gnosis, consisting of the innate, enjoyment, and emanation bodies, unified as one in the gnosis-mind-speech-body, abides throughout the three worlds— heaven, earth, and the underworld—
and is difficult for those of meager merit to attain among all phenomena.
"Beginning, middle, and end" means that which is established throughout the past, future, and present times; thus it is called "established in beginning, middle, and end."
The commentary on CS 5: [The fire arises] from the conjunction of the wood to be rubbed and the rubbing stick, accompanied by the recitation of mantras and other such rites.
Thus:

here, that very gnosis arises for yogins through the union of the two organs by means of the friction of the churned and the churning stick; likewise, there is yoga as previously described, and the knowledge of ritual, which is worldly.
Knowledge through ritual is accomplished by the recitation of mantras and by the meditation on the mandala-circle.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is indicated that [the goal] is accomplished through mantras, fire offerings (*homādi*), and the like.

That very knowledge is "knowledge of the ritual" (*vidhijñāna*) and "worldly knowledge. Thus, both the yoga previously mentioned—which consists of emptiness and compassion—and, by the word "and," the knowledge of the ritual taught in the *Lakṣābhidhāna-tantra* by me, are now [taught] in this concise tantra, the *Vajravārāhī*.
"Listen to this tantra, which is being taught as the most essential of the essential"—

thus, the relationship between the teacher and the requester, together with the relationship between the subject matter and its expression, has been elucidated by the commentary according to the definitive rule of the Blessed One through both the interpretable and the definitive meanings.
(13) Chapter III: The Worship of the Kulikā. Commentary on CS 6ABC. Now, the worship of the Kulikā is described by the passage beginning with “by the central and supreme breath,” and so forth.
Here, the *madhyamā* is the *avadhūtī*, the channel flowing with the line of fire (*agnirekhā*) between *Ālikāli*.

Among its breaths—numbering twenty-one thousand six hundred per day and night—there are six hundred and seventy-five breaths corresponding to the transitions through the twelve zodiacal signs (*lagna*) during one day and night.
The remaining ones, numbering twenty-two thousand nine hundred and fifty, flow through the *lalanā* and *rasanā* in the twelve zodiacal signs (*dvādaśalagna*).
Among them, in each odd sign beginning with Aries (*meṣa*), eighteen hundred breaths flow through the *lalanā*;
likewise, in each even sign beginning with Taurus (*vṛṣabha*), [eighteen hundred] flow through the *rasanā*.

Of those two, at the time of each respective transition (*saṃkrānti*), there are fifty-six and a quarter breaths in the middle of the even and odd lunar mansions (*lagna*) belonging to the central *avadhūtī*.

These are inferior, bringing death to living beings; they arise from the time of Kulikā, have a perishable nature, and cause untimely death (*ariṣṭa-maraṇa*) because they flow as the fire of time (*kālāgni*).
The remaining one thousand eight hundred breaths, minus those fifty-six and a quarter, flow through the five mandalas of the *lalanā* and *rasanā*.
In each of these, there are three hundred and sixty channels carrying the *maṇḍalas*, which are less than eleven and a quarter breaths [in duration].
Here, the five *maṇḍalas* beginning with space belong to the *lalanā*;

the five beginning with earth belong to the *rasanā* on the left and right. Here, in the petals of the navel-lotus, they are situated respectively in the center, east, south, north, and west as the *maṇḍalas* of space, wind, fire, water, and earth.
In the pericarp is the sixth, the mandala of gnosis (the equinox).

Above the two nostrils, as follows: in the middle, above, on the right, and on the left, and below, respectively, there is the sequence beginning with *śūnya* on the left and beginning with *bhūmi* on the right.
The sixth [cycle] consists of fifty-six breaths plus one-quarter, occurring simultaneously in both nostrils.

(14) When the breaths flowing through the left and right channels of these mandalas are made to enter the central *avadhūtī* channel—either by the power of shifting the flow between the channels or by the power of *prāṇāyāma*—they become "common" (*sādhāraṇa*), meaning they deceive the signs of untimely death.
By the power of yoga, they flow within the central channel.

Here, the supreme [winds], produced from the great vital breath (*mahāprāṇa*), destroy those that are inferior and common; they bestow the bliss of the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara-sukha*); they are to be personally realized by the wisdom of the yogi; they are devoid of the nature of the pleasure derived from the objects of the external senses;

they are accessible to the divine senses; they are measured by the number of the cycles of breath; and they consist of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) because of the non-emission of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
In each of those, the breath of supreme unchanging bliss is the "supreme-middle breath" (*madhyamottamaśvāsa*); by means of that supreme-middle breath,
together with scented water— here, "scent" refers to the *lalanā*, which flows as the downward and upward breath of Vairocana-candra.

"Water" refers to the *rasanā*, which flows with urine, solar breath, and downward-moving wind, located below and above; "middle" refers to the *avadhūtī*, which flows with semen, menstrual blood, Rāhu, and the fire of time (*kālāgni*), located below and above. Within this middle *avadhūtī*, the lowest exhaling breath bestows death upon living beings.
The common [breath] is the "deceiver of untimely death" (*ariṣṭamaraṇavañcaka*), which is middling.
The supreme [breath], which bestows the bliss of the ultimate syllable (*paramākṣara*) and grants the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, is therefore called the "middling-supreme breath.

That very [breath], joined below and above with the channels of feces, urine, moon, and sun, becomes of one flavor (*samarasībhūta*) with the channels of semen, blood, Rāhu, and the fire of time; it sustains the four drops of bodhicitta and is the unification of body, speech, and mind.
"Ūrdhvaretā ekaśūkavajra" means:

by that middle and supreme breath, accompanied by scented water, having the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), free from subject and object, the great breath of the Vajradhara, devoid of the causes of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*), arisen from the cause of the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), and personally experienced through the gnosis of the yogi—[this is] the poison... (15)

By means of that which has become one with the senses, through the blazing Caṇḍālī at the navel, by the nectar melted from the moon at the forehead— the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of which have been incinerated— and by that which flows upward without falling, arising as the innate body (*sahajakāya*) born of the supreme syllable, devoid of the sounds *ali*, *kāli*, *hūṃ*, and *phaṭ*, free from the meditation on the maṇḍala circle, beyond the empowerment of mantra-recitation and mudrās, outside the dharma of following the guru’s command, non-abiding in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and inseparable from compassion and emptiness— from the forehead...

By means of the great non-emission of passion (*mahācyutarāga*), in the form of uninterrupted drops of bodhicitta extending as far as the *vajramaṇi*, through the middle and supreme breaths— one should constantly worship the *kulikā*.

Here, the *kulikā* is the central *avadhūtī*, Vajravārāhī, free from obscurations, devoid of subject and object, the destroyer of the host of Māras for yogins, and [the destroyer] of the collection of aggregates, elements, and sense-bases for the ignorant.
And she who causes the destruction of the *bodhicitta*— bestowing death through the emission of the *bodhicitta*—

is that Vajrayoginī, who is the mere appearance of one’s own mind, the Mahāmudrā, endowed with all excellent aspects, the Perfection of Wisdom, Emptiness, Suchness, the Kulikā, and is called the Lotus (*padma*).

One should [worship] that Kulikā with the supreme unchanging bliss, by means of the drop of *bodhicitta* which does not fall, which is like molten moon, which is great passion, which is the supreme central breath, and which is accompanied by scented water produced from the Kulikā.
By that means, one should worship that very self-prajñā.

The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is that the yogi should effect the unity of the apprehended and the apprehending mind, of the object of knowledge and the knowing consciousness, and of emptiness and compassion.

"One should worship constantly" means at all times—whether impure or pure, standing or sitting, sleeping or engaged in the activities of body, speech, and mind—one remains devoted to supreme unchanging bliss, free from longing for the enjoyment of all sensual desires.
Externally, one is attached to the enjoyment of sense objects perceived by the divine senses.

Thus, the Blessed One has taught that the ritual for the worship of the Kulikā through the medium and superior breaths is for the sake of attaining the Mahāmudrā-siddhi by means of supramundane truth.

(16) Chapter IV: The Worship of the *Dūtikās*. Commentary on CS 6D. Now, for the sake of accomplishing worldly attainments (*laukikasiddhi*), the procedure for the worship of the *dūtikās*—both externally and internally—is described according to specific times and so forth, by means of the wheel of the movement of the *dūtīs* at the *melāpaka*, using the pill of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛtagulikā*) in battle; [using] those slain by weapons who are blameless, or those dead through accident, or those killed in evil deeds, or [remnants of] cow-sacrifices and the like, which are the great pledges (*mahāsamaya*), along with the five offerings and so forth. It begins with the words "at a specific time" and so on.
Time and its Subdivisions: Appropriate Moments for the Performance of a Rite In this regard, time is twofold: external and internal.
It is further divided according to the year and the day, respectively.
Its specific distinction consists of the specific distinctions of time, both externally and internally.

The external specific distinction of time is the zodiacal circle consisting of the twelve ascendants (*dvādaśalagna*). Here, within that [external sphere], the specific distinctions of time for each year are further [divided into] days, fortnights, months, seasons, *yugas*, ages, and solstices (*ayana*).

Furthermore, the specific divisions of time within the internal [body] are: breaths, water-measures (*pānīyapala*), *ghaṭikās*, *muhūrtas*, half-watches (*ardhaprahara*), ascendants (*lagna*), watches (*prahara*), twilights (*saṃdhyā*), and day-and-night (*ahorātra*). As for the specific divisions of time externally, they are: thirty-sixty days (*dināni*) per year, twenty-four fortnights (*pakṣa*), twelve months (*māsa*), six seasons (*ṛtu*), four *yugas* consisting of three months each, three periods (*kāla*) consisting of four months each, and two solstices (*ayana*) consisting of six months each.
The collection of these constitutes one year, which is "time" (*kāla*); within the internal self (*adhyātman*), this is "time" for each day.

There are twenty-one thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations; three thousand six hundred *pānīyapala* measures of water; sixty *ghaṭikās*; thirty *muhūrtas*; sixteen half-watch periods (*ardhaprahara*); twelve zodiacal signs (*lagna*);
eight watch periods (*prahara*); and four [fortnights]. (17)
Twilight and day-and-night—this collection constitutes one day, which is time.
Thus, just as there is a specific division of time through the movement of the sun externally, so too is there a specific division of time through the movement of the vital breath internally.
By means of that specific division of time, one should worship the female messengers (dūtī) every year and every day.
The female messengers (dūtikās) are the thirty-six yoginīs beginning with Vajraḍākinī and ending with Yamamathanī; one should worship them.

In this context, just as the female messengers (dūtī) are to be worshipped, so too are the innate accomplished ones (sahaja-siddhāḥ)—the twenty-four [deities] beginning with Vajrasattva, categorized as inferior, middling, and superior—worshipped in reverse order, because they bestow the accomplishments (siddhi) of the subterranean, the terrestrial, and the celestial within the wheels of body, speech, and mind.
They too are to be worshipped at specific times; such is the rule of the Tathāgatas.

In this way, one should worship the female messengers (*dūtī*), the innate ones (*sahajā*), and the accomplished ones (*siddhāḥ*) with the pill of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta-gulikā*), with the meats of the cow, dog, and so forth, with blameless sacramental substances (*samaya*), and with the five offerings and so on, in the external *gaṇacakra*.
Internally, in the wheels of gnosis, mind, speech, and body, there is a specific time by means of the movement of the sun and the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
By that specific time, there is the movement of the female messengers.
Through the movement of the messengers (dūtī), there is the enjoyment, dissolution, and authority of the Kulikā and the thirty-six messengers.
In the present time, there is enjoyment according to the sequence;
in the future time, there is dissolution and authority.
In the past time there is authority;
at sunrise there is enjoyment;
at midday there is authority.
Mastery resides in the place where [the breath] has set;
the principle is that dissolution occurs at midnight.
Thus, the movement of the Yoginīs takes place externally on the day of enjoyment and internally during the time of enjoyment.
Through the movement of the Yoginīs, there is the gathering of the wheels (*cakramelāpaka*).
At the gathering of the wheels, one should worship her who enjoys the day and her who enjoys the time (*velā*).
This is the enjoyment during the stage of childhood.
In youth there is authority;
in old age there is sovereignty;
at the time of death, at midnight, there is dissolution.
Furthermore, arising from dissolution is called "the fool. Thus, by means of specific times—

through the division of the four twilights (*catuḥsaṃdhyā*), the division of the eight watches (*prahara*), and the division of the twenty-four fortnights— there is everywhere a fixed rule regarding the authority over enjoyment and dissolution, as well as the sovereignty, of the thirty-six yoginīs according to their respective times.

The worship of the four Jñānacakra-Ḍākinīs is now described. Here, for the sake of attaining Mahāmudrā-siddhi, the mantra-practitioner should at all times worship Kulikā Vajravārāhī—whether externally or internally—with the supreme central breath characterized by great immutable bliss (*mahākṣarasukha*).
For the sake of worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*), [one should worship] Vajraḍākinī and the others in their proper sequence according to specific times. (18)
"One should worship" means as follows:

here, externally, at the transition of Capricorn (*makara-saṃkrānti*), when the eastern face arises, one should worship Vajraḍākinī for the sake of accomplishing the rite of slaying (*māraṇa*). At the transition of Aries (*meṣa-saṃkrānti*), when the southern face arises, one should worship Lāmā for the sake of accomplishing the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*).
During the transition into Cancer (karkaṭasaṃkrānti), at the rising of the western face, one should worship Kaṇḍarohā for the purpose of paralyzing (stambhana).
During the transition into Libra (tulāsaṃkrānti), at the rising of the northern face, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should worship Rūpiṇī for the purpose of pacification (śāntika).

At the end of the three months of each of these three transitions, there are the junctions of the four ages (caturyugasandhyā) of the year, distinguished by the increase or decrease of the sun’s wealth and debt.

On their respective days of transition (*saṃkrānti*), according to the stated sequence, the four *ḍākinīs* who are *bhoginīs* are the goddesses of the East, South, West, and North of the Blessed One, distinguished by the divisions of the Body, Speech, Mind, and Wisdom.
They are for the purpose of accomplishing the rites of slaying and so forth; it is a fixed rule that this is not by means of the differentiation of the elements such as earth and the rest.
Thus, in every case where the expansion of activities is to be accomplished as will be described, this is the rule for worship according to the division of faces.

Now, the worship of the eight Śmaśānadevīs is described. Here, on the day of the Makara-saṃkrānti, one worships Kākāsyā for the purpose of eradication (uccāṭana); at midday, one worships Ulūkāsyā for the purpose of attraction (ākṛṣṭi).
On the day of the Aries transit (*meṣa-saṃkrānti*), one should nail Śvānāsyā for the purpose of immobilization;
on the day of the Taurus half-transit (*vṛṣabha-ardhadina*), one should nail Śūkarāsyā for the purpose of nourishment;
and on the day of the Cancer transit (*karkaṭa-saṃkrānti*), one should nail Yamadāḍhī for the purpose of neutralizing poison.

The yogi should worship Yamādūtī for the purpose of enchanting during the half-day of Leo; Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī for the purpose of paralyzing on the day of the Libra transit (tulā-saṃkrānti); and Yamamathanī for the purpose of creating enmity during the half-day of Scorpio. Thus, there are eight watches (praharas) in a year consisting of one and a half months each.
In those initial days, according to the stated sequence, the eight Yoginīs, who are the enjoyers, [remain] for one and a half months each; such is the rule.
(19) The Worship of the Twenty-four Vīras and Vīreśvarīs of the Citta-, Vāk-, and Kāya-cakras Now, the worship of the goddesses of the citta-, vāk-, and kāya-cakras is described.

Here, on the new moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, one worships Pracaṇḍā and Kaṇṭhakapālin for the sake of accomplishing rites of slaying (*māraṇa*). And on the full moon day, one worships Caṇḍākṣī and Mahākaṅkāla for the sake of subjugation (*viśya*).
On the new moon of Puṣya, one should worship Prabhāvatī and Kaṅkāla for the purpose of immobilization;
on the full moon, Mahānāsā and Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin for the purpose of nourishment;
and on the new moon of Māgha, Vīramatī and Surāvairin for the purpose of pacification.

On the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, one should worship Kharvarī and Amitābha for the purpose of enchanting; on the new moon day of Phālguna, Laṅkeśvarī and Vajraprabha for the purpose of attracting;
and on the full moon day [of Caitra], Drumacchāyā and Vajradeha for the purpose of creating enmity.
Thus, during the eight days of the fortnights of the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, the eight Heroines and Heroines of the Mind Wheel are to be worshipped according to the stated sequence.
Now the worship of the wheel of speech is described.
Here, on the new moon day of Caitra, one worships Airāvatī and Aṅkurika for the purpose of eradication;
on the full moon day, one worships Mahābhairavā and Vajrajaṭila for the purpose of causing affliction.
On the new moon of Vaiśākha, one should worship Vāyuvegā and Mahāvīra for the purpose of paralyzing the enemy army;
on the full moon, Surābhakṣī and Vajrahuṃkāra for the purpose of causing rain from the clouds;
and on the new moon of Jyeṣṭha, Śyāmadevī and Subhadra for the purpose of pacifying fever.

On the full moon of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship Subhadrā and Vajrabhadra for the purpose of splitting the underworld (pātāla). On the new moon of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship Hayakarṇā and Mahābhairava for the purpose of inducing possession (āveśa).
On the full moon, one should worship Khagānanā and Virūpākṣa for the purpose of dispersing the clouds.

On the eighth days of the fortnights during the four months beginning with Caitra, according to the stated sequence, the eight heroes and heroines, or the *bhoginīs*, reside in the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*).
Now the worship of the body wheel (*kāyacakra*) is described.

Here, on the new moon of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should [worship] Cakravegā and Mahābala for the sake of accomplishing the great sword (*mahākhaḍga*). On the full moon, one should [worship] Khaṇḍarohā and Ratnavajra for the sake of subjugating the daughters of the *nāgas*.
On the new moon of Bhādrapada, one worships Śauṇḍinī and Hayagrīva for the purpose of paralyzing the serpent kings;
on the full moon, Cakravarmiṇī and Ākāśagarbha for the purpose of accomplishing the great elixir;
and on the new moon of Āśvina, Suvīrā and Heruka for the purpose of accomplishing the fruit of immortality.
On the full moon day, one should worship Mahābalā and Padmanarteśvara for the sake of accomplishing material wealth (*dravya*).

On the new moon day of Kārtika, one should worship Cakravartinī and Vairocana for the sake of accomplishing jewels (*ratna*). On the full moon day, one should worship Mahāvīryā and Vajrasattva for the sake of shaking the three worlds (*trailokyaprakampana*). Thus, on the eighth days of the fortnights during the four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, the eight Heroines (*vīreśvarī*) and Heroines (*vīrā*) are the *bhoginīs* [to be worshipped] according to the stated sequence.
In the body wheel.
Alternatively, on the day of the transition of Scorpio, during the half-period of Scorpio;
on the day of the transition of Sagittarius, during the half-period of Sagittarius;
on the day of the transition of Capricorn, during the half-period of Capricorn.
During the transit of Aquarius and during the half-days of Aquarius, the eight Vīras and Vīreśvarīs are the Bhoginīs in the Citta-cakra.
Likewise, during the transit of Pisces and the half [of Pisces];
during the transit of Aries and the half [of Aries]; and during the transit of Taurus and the half [of Taurus].
During the transit of Gemini and during the half-day of Gemini—

on these eight days, according to the stated sequence, the eight Vīras and Vīreśvarīs, or the Bhoginīs, reside in the Vākcakra. Likewise, during the transit of Cancer and during the half-day of Cancer.
During the Leo transit, in the first half of Leo;
during the Virgo transit, in the first half of Virgo;
during the Libra transit, in the first half of Libra.
During these eight days, the eight Vīravīreśvarīs, the Bhoginīs, reside in the body wheel (*kāyacakra*) in their respective order.
Here, the first year currently occurring—divided into three-year periods starting from *prabhava*—is to be taken; namely:
*prabhava*, *vibhava*, *śukla*, *pramoda*, and *prajāpati*.
Aṅgiras, Śrīmukha, Bhāva, Yuvan, and likewise Dhātṛ.
Īśvara, Bahudhanya, Pramādī, Vikrama, Vṛṣa,
Citrabhānu, Subhānu, Tāraṇa, Pārthiva, and Avyaya.
Sarvajit, Sarvadhārī, Virodhin, Vikṛta, Khara,
Nandana, Vijaya, Jaya, Manmatha, and Durmukha.
Hemalamba, Vilambi, Vikari, Sharvari, Plava,
Shubhakrit, Shobhana, Krodhi, Vishvavasu, and Parabhava.
Pravaṅga, Kīlaka, Saumya, Sādhāraṇa, Virodhakṛt,
Paridhāvī, Pramādī, Ānanda, Rākṣasa, and Anala.
Piṅgala, Kāladūtī, Siddhārtha, Raudra, Durmati,
Dundubhi, Rudhirodgārī, Raktākṣī, Krodhana, and Kṣaya.
Thus are the sixty-year cycles.
At the end of three years, the first triad of years is to be taken again according to the division of the three qualities (*guṇa*);
therein, during the first year, one should recite the mantra of the four-faced one (*caturvaktra*) together with the names of the four goddesses, divided into periods of three months each.
Then, in the second year, one should recite the eight-syllable mantra accompanied by the names of the eight yoginīs, according to the division of one and a half months.
Then, in the third year, for the sake of accomplishing the previously mentioned *karmaprasara*, one should recite the limb-by-limb *mālāmantra* accompanied by the names of the twenty-four goddesses.

Thus, having accomplished the thirty-six ḍākinīs through three years, six years, nine years, twelve years, or thirty-six years, the mantra practitioner thereafter performs the expansion of all activities and the means for attaining mundane siddhis;

such is the rule of the Tathāgata. Likewise, within the internal [system], there are four junctions (*saṃdhyā*), eight watches (*prahara*), [periods] consisting of two and a half *daṇḍas*, and twenty-four lunar fortnights of zodiacal signs (*lagna*).
At these times, every day, one should worship Vajraḍākinī and the others in order to accomplish the previously mentioned siddhis.
This is the rule for the procedure of worshipping the messenger (dūtī) according to the specific times.
The Subdivisions of Time According to Other Tantras: Now, the specific divisions of time mentioned in other tantras will be described.
In this context, the Blessed One has taught these specific divisions of time in various tantras;
here, they are presented merely by way of summary.
And that [point] should be understood here according to the intention expressed by him elsewhere, because of the Tathāgata’s statement: "A tantra is to be understood by means of another tantra."
Thus is that specific division of time:
first, those zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn (*makara*) in the four seats (*catuṣpīṭha*) are the twelve *nāḍīs* beginning with Rohiṇī;
and those twelve months beginning with Puṣya are the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga*) beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, externally and internally, there are twelve zodiac signs (lagnas) for each year and each day;
each individual sign consists of five *daṇḍas*,
and one *daṇḍa* consists of sixty *pānīyapalas*.
A *panīpala* consists of six breaths (*śvāsa*).
Thus, in one day and night, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations; externally these are the *daṇḍas* of the Sun, and internally they are the breaths.
Such is the reckoning for one day and night.
Likewise, it was stated by the Blessed One in the *Hevajra*: "In the *nirmāṇacakra*, there are sixty-four *daṇḍas* consisting of five hundred and twenty-five *pala* of water;
in the *mahāsukhacakra*, there are thirty-two *ghaṭikās* consisting of two *daṇḍas* each;
and in the *saṃbhogacakra*, there are sixteen transits (*saṃkrānti*) consisting of two *ghaṭikās* each."
In the *Dharmacakra*, there are eight watches (*prahara*), each consisting of four *ghatikās*.
Here, the instruction of the Guru is that [the sequence] for the *Saṃbhoga* is reversed in the *Mahāsukhacakra*.
Thus, the specific divisions of time within a day and night are summarized in another *Laghutantra*.
Furthermore, it was taught by the Blessed One in greater detail in the *Lakṣābhidhāna* and other root tantras,
as follows:
"In that regard, externally, for the sun, there is exactly one day per year."
On that day, there is a specific division of time:
twenty-one thousand six hundred *daṇḍas*, which are the breaths of the sun; and these are the breaths of embodied beings within the self on each respective day.
Thus, the thirty days plus sixty [days] consist of sixty-sixty *daṇḍas* externally, and consist of sixty-sixty breaths internally.
Likewise, the twenty-four fortnights consist of nine hundred nine-hundred *daṇḍas* externally, and consist of nine hundred nine-hundred breaths internally.
Similarly, the twelve months consist of eighteen hundred eighteen-hundred *daṇḍas* externally.
Internally, they consist of eighteen hundred and eighteen hundred breaths each.
Externally, the six seasons consist of thirty-six hundred and thirty-six hundred cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*) each;
internally, they consist of thirty-six hundred and thirty-six hundred breaths each.
Externally, there are four *yugas*, each consisting of five thousand four hundred and fifty-four *daṇḍas*;
internally, they consist of five thousand four hundred and fifty-four breaths (*śvāsa*).
Externally, there are three *kālās*, each consisting of seven thousand two hundred and seventy-two *daṇḍas*.
Internally, they consist of seventy-two hundred and seventy-two hundred breaths.
Externally, each solstice consists of ten thousand eight hundred *daṇḍas*,
and internally, each consists of ten thousand eight hundred breaths.
Thus, in one day and night, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred *daṇḍas* for the sun externally each day;
internally, for embodied beings, these are the breaths (*śvāsa*) each respective day.
Herein, a single inhalation and exhalation of humans constitutes a day and night for the swarms of worms born from the body.
In this very context, this distinction of time is to be understood:
what is one month for humans here is one day and night for the *pretas*.
Sixty years of the Dānavas constitute one year of the Suras;
this is known as a single day and night for the Bodhisattvas, measured by the number of breaths in a cycle.
That very [period] is a day.
"A single breath [is for] the sake of accomplishing the welfare of beings for the Master.
Thus, this specific time should be understood by all every day; it was spoken thus by the Tathāgata in various tantras and other scriptures.
In this way, the specific times for the *Cakrasaṃvara* [practice] should be understood through the *Catuṣpīṭha* and other [tantras],
because they are not heard in the *Mūlatantra*.

By means of this tantra, the movement of the yoginīs (*yoginīsaṃcāra*) and the authority regarding enjoyment and dissolution (*bhogalaya*) in the *Catuṣpīṭha* and others should be understood by the wise.
The rule for the procedure of worship, both externally and internally, according to specific times.

(27) Chapter VI: The Places of the Yoginīs. Now, the locations for the movement of the Yoginīs at the external and internal *pīṭhas* and so forth are described.
Externally, on the summit of Mount Sumeru, in the central courtyard of the Viśvapada;
internally, in the secret lotus at the root-seat (*mūlapīṭha*), Vajravārāhī is the Kulikā.
In the eastern petal of the lotus, within the heart-lotus at the seat of the self (ātmapīṭha), is Vajraḍākinī;
in the southern petal, within the throat-lotus at the seat of the other (parapīṭha), is Lāmā;
in the western petal, within the navel-lotus at the seat of mantra (mantrapīṭha), is Khaṇḍarohā.
On the northern petal of the forehead lotus, at the Tattva-pīṭha, is Rūpiṇī;
in the pericarp of the crown lotus, at the Sarva-pīṭha, Śrī Heruka is to be worshipped in the Jñāna-cakra.
Then, in the sky of the Citta-cakra, in the eight directions of Meru, on the eastern spoke at Pūrṇagiri, upon the head, is Pracaṇḍā with Kaṇḍakapālika.
On the southern spoke at Jālandhara, on the crest-lock, is Caṇḍākṣī and Mahākaṅkāla;
on the western spoke at Oḍḍiyāṇa, above the right ear, is Prabhāvatī and Kaṅkāla;

on the northern spoke at Arbuda, on the back of the neck and the crown of the head, is Mahānāsā and Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrī—these are the Heroes and Heroines, the Enjoyers (Bhoginīs) in the four seats, arranged by the clockwise rotation of the Kundalinī.
Then, on the Īśāna spoke at Godāvarī, above the left ear, is Vīramatī with Surāvairin;
on the Vāyavya spoke at Rāmeśvara, between the eyebrows, is Kharvarī with Amitābha;
on the Nairṛtya spoke at Devīkoṭa, on the two eyes, is Laṅkeśvarī with Vajraprabha.
On the eastern spoke (āgneyāra) in Mālavaka, [one should worship] Drumacchāyā and Vajradeha at the two armpits.

Thus, in these four secondary seats (upapīṭhas), the Bhoginīs—along with the Vīras and Vīreśvarīs—are to be worshipped by means of a counter-clockwise rotation starting from the left ear-ring (*kuṇḍalāvāmāvarta*).
In this manner, one should worship the Bhoginīs of the seats and secondary seats, who are the Sky-farers (*khecaryas*), within the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*).
Then, on the circle of the earth, in the eight directions from Meru, in the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*): at Kāmarūpa on the eastern spoke, in the two armpits, are Airāvatī and Aṅkurika;
at Oḍra on the southern spoke, in the pair of breasts, are Mahābhairavā and Vajrajaṭila.
Thus, in the two fields, there are the two *bhoginīs*, Savīra and Vīreśvarī.
In the western spoke, at the navel, are Triśakuni and Vāyuvegā-Mahāvīra.
In the northern spoke, at the tip of the nose, are Kośala and Surābhakṣī-Vajrahūṃkāra.
Thus, at the two secondary fields (*upakṣetra*), there are the two *bhoginīs* Savīra and Vīreśvarī.

In this manner, the *bhoginīs* of the fields and secondary fields proceed by a clockwise rotation starting from Kuṇḍala. Then, on the eastern spoke (*īśānāra*) in Kaliṅga, at the mouth, are Śyāmādevī and Subhadra.
On the western spoke, in Lampāka, at the throat, are Subhadrā and Vajraprabha; these are the two *bhoginīs* together with the Hero and the Mistress of Heroes in the two *chandohas*.
On the southwestern spoke, in Kāñcī, at the heart, are Hayakarṇā and Mahābhairava.
On the southeastern spoke, in Himālaya, at the genitals, are Khagānanā and Virūpākṣa.

Thus, in the *upachandoha* [of the speech-chakra], there are the two *bhoginīs*, Savīra and Vīreśvarī; these are the *bhoginīs* of the *chandoha* and *upachandoha*. In this manner, the *kṣetra*, *upakṣetra*, *chandoha*, and *upachandoha* *bhoginīs*, who move upon the earth (*bhūcarī*), are to be worshipped by the practitioner in the speech-chakra (*vākcakra*) according to the counter-clockwise rotation starting from Kuṇḍalā. Then, on the surface of the earth within the oceanic circle, in the eight directions from Meru, in the body-chakra (*kāyacakre*), at the eastern spoke in Pretapurī, at the *liṅga*, are Cakravegā and Mahābala.
On the southern spoke, at Gṛhadevatā, is Khaṇḍarohā and Ratnavajra;
thus, in these two meeting places (melāpaka), the two goddesses Bhoginī are accompanied by the Vīra and Vīreśvarī.
On the western spoke, at Saurāṣṭra, on the pair of thighs, are Śauṇḍinī and Hayagrīva.
On the northern spoke, in Suvarṇadvīpa, on the two shanks, are Cakravarmiṇī and Ākāśagarbha.
Thus, in the two secondary meeting places (upamelāpaka), there are the two female enjoyers (bhoginī) along with the hero and the mistress of heroes (vīravīreśvarī).
In this way, the female enjoyers of the meeting places and secondary meeting places follow the clockwise rotation of the earrings.
Then, in the city on the northeast spoke, [one places] Suvīra and Heruka on the toes;
in the northwest spoke, in Sindhu, [one places] Mahābala and Padmanarteśvara on the tops of the feet.
Thus, in these two cremation grounds, there are the two *bhoginīs*, Vīrā and Vīreśvarī.
In the southwest spoke, at Maru, on the two big toes, are Cakravartinī and Vairocana;
in the southeast spoke, at Kulatā, on the two knees, are Mahāvīryā and Vajrasattva—thus, in the two secondary cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*), are the two *bhoginī*s, Sarvīrā and Vīreśvarī.
In this manner, the *bhoginī*s of the cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) and secondary cremation grounds proceed by the counter-clockwise rotation of Kuṇḍalā.

In this way, the goddesses of the *melāpaka*, *upamelāpaka*, *śmaśāna*, and *upaśmaśāna* who enjoy the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*) are to be worshipped through the movement of the yoginīs in the assembly of the wheels (*cakramelāpaka*), according to the sequence to be described. Thus concludes the worship of the movement through the three wheels.

Then, in the netherworld (*pātala*), within the circle of fire and wind, in the eight directions from Meru, in the great hell of Intense Smoke (*tīvradhūma*) and in the eight great cremation grounds (*mahāśmaśāna*):
there, in the eastern cremation ground, Śūlabheda, at the mouth-gate is Kākāsyā;
in the south, at the corpse-burning ground, at the right nostril is Ulūkāsyā.
In the west, at the anus, which has the odor of putrefaction,
is Śvānāsyā; in the north, at the nostrils, which have the odor of moisture, is Śūkarāsyā.
Thus, by the clockwise rotation starting from Kuṇḍalā:
then, in the northeast spoke, at the door of the left ear, is Bālamṛtyu; Yamadāḍhī is in the northwest, at the door of the right ear, for the bite of a serpent; Yamadūtī is in the southwest.

In the southwest, at the door of the right eye, is Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī during the terrible battle; in the southeast, at the door of the left eye, is Yamamathanī during the Ucchiṣṭa [rite]. Thus, by the counter-clockwise rotation of the earrings, and likewise by the clockwise and counter-clockwise rotations—whether in direct or reverse order—the goddesses who enjoy the eight great cremation grounds are to be worshipped in the *cakramelāpaka*.
Thus, there are gatekeepers at the navel, heart, throat, and forehead—the wheels of gnosis, mind, speech, and body—as well as at the eight gates beginning with the mouth.
In this way, there are thirty-six yoginīs, both externally and internally; such is the instruction on their locations.
(30) Chapter VII: On Enjoyment, Dissolution, Authority, and Sovereignty.
(31) Now, enjoyment, dissolution, authority, and sovereignty are explained with respect to the Kulikas and others.

In this context, for the Kulikā, there are everywhere the enjoyments (*bhoga*), absorptions (*laya*), and authorities (*adhikāra*), as well as sovereignty (*prabhutva*) over her own seat (*ātmapīṭha*) and the others.
For Vajraḍākinī and the others, these correspond respectively to their own seats and so forth.
Here, enjoyment resides in one's own seat, while absorption occurs in another’s seat.
In the seat of reality (tattvapīṭha) there is authority;
in the seat of mantra (mantrapīṭha) there is sovereignty;
in the supreme seat (parapīṭha) there is enjoyment, and in the seat of mantra there is dissolution.
In the seat of the self (ātmapīṭha) there is authority; in the seat of reality (tattvapīṭha), sovereignty;
and in the seat of mantra (mantrapīṭha), enjoyment.
Dissolution occurs in the seat of reality (tattvapīṭha);
authority in the supreme seat (parapīṭha);
sovereignty in the seat of the self (ātmapīṭha), and enjoyment in the seat of reality.
Dissolution occurs in the seat of the self (*ātmapīṭha*);
authority in the seat of mantra (*mantrapīṭha*); and sovereignty in the supreme seat (*parapīṭha*).

Thus, through the division of the four junctions (*catuḥsaṃdhyā*), the movement of the messenger (*dūtī*) in the assembly of the wheel (*cakramelāpaka*) proceeds clockwise in the navel, at the wheel of knowledge (*jñānacakra*).

enjoyment is in Jālandhara;
dissolution is in Oḍḍiyāṇa.

lordship is at Arbuda;
enjoyment is at Oḍḍiyāṇa.
Absorption is at Arbuda;
authority is at Jālandhara;
sovereignty is at Pūrṇagiri.
In Arbuda is enjoyment;
in Pūrṇagiri is dissolution;
in Oḍḍiyāṇa is authority.

Sovereignty is in Jālandhara; thus, by the rightward coil of the Kuṇḍalinī, during the rising of Scorpio and its half, the rising of Sagittarius and its half, on the new moon or full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, or on the new moon or full moon of Puṣya, the movement of the Yoginīs occurs in the heart at the Citta-cakra. sovereignty over Devīkoṭa.

in Devīkoṭa is dissolution (laya);
in the Godāvarī is mastery (adhikāra).

enjoyment at Devīkoṭa;
dissolution in Mālava. (32)

lordship over the Godāvarī; enjoyment in Mālava.

authority at Devīkoṭa;
sovereignty at Rāmeśvara.

Thus, by the counter-clockwise rotation of Kuṇḍalā, there is the movement of the Yoginīs in the half-Makara at the rising of Makara, and in the half-Kumbha at the rising of Kumbha; this occurs in the Heart, which is the Citta-cakra.

Or, externally, it is the *cakramelāpaka* (the gathering of the wheels) in the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) and secondary seats (*upapīṭhas*), where the movement of the Yoginīs takes place in the Citta-cakra.
Here, when enjoyment occurs in Kāmarūpa—
Then there is dissolution in Oḍra,
authority in Kośala,
and sovereignty in Triśakuni.
Thus, enjoyment is in Oḍra;
dissolution is in Triśakuni;
and authority is in Kāmarūpa.
In Kośala there is sovereignty;
in Triśakuni there is enjoyment; in Kośala there is dissolution.
In Oḍra there is authority;
in Kāmarūpa, sovereignty;
in Kośala, enjoyment.
Absorption in Kāmarūpa; authority in Triśakuni;
sovereignty in Oḍra.

Thus, the movement of the Yoginīs in the external *melāpaka* at the throat, the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*), by way of the rightward rotation of the *kuṇḍalī*, consists of the *kṣetra*s and *upakṣetra*s.
[This occurs] during the rising of Pisces and the half of Pisces, and during the rising of Aries and the half of Aries, for the Yoginīs.
Here, when there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) in Kaliṅga, there is dissolution (*laya*) in Lampāka.
In the Himalayas there is authority; in Kāñcī there is sovereignty, and likewise in Lampāka there is enjoyment; in Kāñcī there is dissolution, and in Kaliṅga there is authority.

enjoyment in Kāñcī;
dissolution in the Himalayas.

lordship over Kaliṅga;
enjoyment in the Himalayas.
Dissolution in Kaliṅga;
authority in Kāñcī;
sovereignty in Lampāka.

Thus, the *Chandohas*, *Upachandohas*, and *Bhoginīs* move by way of the counter-clockwise rotation of Kuṇḍalā during the rising of Taurus and the half of Taurus, and during the rising of Gemini and the half of Gemini, in the throat, that is, in the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*), at the external assembly of wheels (*cakramelāpaka*). Here, when there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) in Pretapurī, there is dissolution (*laya*) in Gṛhadevatā.
There is authority over Suvarṇadvīpa and sovereignty over Saurāṣṭra; likewise,
there is enjoyment with the domestic deity and dissolution in Saurāṣṭra.

his sovereignty is over Suvarṇadvīpa;
his enjoyment is in Saurāṣṭra.

authority over the household deity;
sovereignty in Pretapurī.

dissolution in Pretapurī;
and authority in Saurāṣṭra.
Sovereignty resides in the household deity.
Thus, the *melāpakas* and *upamelāpakas*, who are the enjoyers (*bhoginīs*), are located in the forehead—the body wheel (*kāyacakra*)—by way of the rightward coil of the *kuṇḍalī*.

During the rising of Cancer and the first half of Cancer, as well as during the rising of Leo and the first half of Leo, the movement of the yoginīs occurs in the external wheel-conjunction (*cakramelāpaka*) within the body wheel.
In this context, when there is enjoyment in the city, then there is dissolution in Sindh; authority in Kulatā;
and sovereignty in Maru.
Thus, enjoyment is in Sindh,
dissolution is in Maru,
and authority is in Nagara.
In Kulatā there is sovereignty;
in Maru there is enjoyment; in Kulatā there is dissolution.
In Sindh, there is authority;
in the city, sovereignty;
in Kulatā, enjoyment.
He has his abode in the city;
he holds authority over the desert;
he possesses sovereignty over the Indus.

Thus, by means of the leftward rotation of the earrings, the movement of the yoginīs occurs in the body wheel (*kāyacakra*) at the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) and secondary cremation ground (*upaśmaśāna*),

during the rising of Virgo (*kanyā*) and the middle of Virgo, as well as during the rising of Libra (*tulā*) and the middle of Libra, on the forehead; this is the meeting (*melāpaka*) in the external wheel within the body wheel.

The movement of these twenty-four yoginīs within the three wheels occurs according to specific times, through the division of the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Scorpio into their respective halves.
Here, when there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) in Śūlabheda, there is dissolution (*laya*) in Śavadahana;
and there is authority (*adhikāra*) in Klinnagandha.
Mastery is in the foul odor;
likewise, enjoyment is in the cremation ground,
and dissolution is in the foul odor.
In Śūlabheda there is authority;
in Klinnagandha there is sovereignty; in Pūtigandha there is enjoyment.
Absorption in the stench of the putrid;
authority over the cremation of corpses;
sovereignty over the piercing by the stake.
In the foul-smelling [state] there is enjoyment;
in the piercing by the trident there is dissolution;
in the putrid-smelling [state] there is authority.
[The goddesses] presiding over the cremation ground and so forth;
thus, by means of the clockwise rotation starting from the right ear,
their movement occurs at midnight through the first, second, third, and fourth watches in the four gates beginning with the mouth, as well as externally in the *gaṇacakra* of the yoginīs.
In this system, when there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) in the death of a child, there is dissolution (*laya*) in a snakebite;
authority (*adhikāra*) resides in the leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*);
and sovereignty (*prabhutva*) resides in a fierce battle—thus, there is enjoyment in a snakebite.
Dissolution occurs in a terrible battle;
authority over the death of children;
and sovereignty over the remnants of food.
In a terrible battle, there is enjoyment;
in what is left over, dissolution;
in being bitten by a snake, authority.
In Bālamṛtyu there is mastery;
in Ucchiṣṭa there is enjoyment;
in Bālamṛtyu there is dissolution.
Authority over fierce battle;
sovereignty over snakebite—
thus are the Kuṇḍalās, who enjoy the cremation grounds of the intermediate directions, arranged in a counter-clockwise rotation.
From midday, during the first, second, third, or fourth watch, there is the movement of the Śmaśānabhoginīs through the four gates beginning with the left ear.
Likewise, in the external *cakramelāpaka*, there is movement through the eight gates beginning with the mouth according to specific times divided into eight watches.
Thus, the movement of the Yoginīs is twofold: externally and internally.
One [set of goddesses] resides in the cardinal directions by means of the four faces of mind, speech, knowledge, and body, following a clockwise rotation starting from Kuṇḍalā.
The other [set] resides in the intermediate directions by means of the faces of body, knowledge, speech, and mind, following a counter-clockwise rotation starting from Kuṇḍalā.

Here, on the eastern petal of the knowledge-lotus, among the spokes of the wheels of mind, speech, and body located in the east and southeast, the *Bhoginīs*—who possess the nature of the faces of mind—reside in the eastern and southeastern great cremation grounds, bestowing the accomplishment of rites such as killing.

Thus, on the southern petal, in the southern and southwestern spokes, and in the southern and southwestern great cremation grounds (*mahāśmaśāna*), the *Bhoginīs*— by virtue of having the nature of the Speech-Face (*vāgvaktra*)— bestow the accomplishment of rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*). Likewise, on the western petal, in the western and northwestern spokes, and in the western and northwestern great cremation grounds, the *Bhoginīs*— by virtue of having the nature of the Knowledge-Face (*jñānavaktra*)— bestow the accomplishment of rites such as paralyzing (*stambhana*).

Likewise, on the northern petal, in the [directions] from North to Northeast, the *Bhoginīs* of the North and Northeast Great Charnel Grounds, by virtue of their nature as Body and Face, shall bestow the accomplishment of rites such as pacification (*śāntika*).

Their seats, which are the mandalas of Wind, Fire, Indra, and Varuṇa produced from the syllables *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*, are to be understood as being respectively located in the heart, throat, navel, and forehead— (34)— upon the backs of their respective vowels.

Thus, according to the division of the four faces of the Blessed One, there is the movement of these [energies] through the specific time determined by the movement of the solar breath; by that specific time, the ritual procedure for worship is established. In this way, in all Yoginītantras, there is a movement according to the specific time measured by the Yoginīs. In the *Mahāmāyā*, there is the movement of the four Yoginīs according to the division of the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*).
Where there are eight Yoginīs, they are [assigned] by way of the division of the eight watches (prahara); where there are sixteen, by way of the division of half-watches;
where there are thirty-two, by way of the division of ghaṭikās;
and where there are sixty-four, by way of the division of daṇḍas.
Where there are fifteen, they are so by way of the division of lunar days (tithi);
where there are twelve, they are so by way of the division of ascendants (lagna);
and where there are twenty-four, they are so by way of the division of half-ascendants (lagnārdha).
Where there are six, they are distinguished by the seasons;
where there are three, they are distinguished by the times of day;
where there are two, they are distinguished by the solstices.
Where there is one [channel], there is no movement;

here, however, everywhere there is a movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) according to the differentiation of the channels. Through this variously differentiated movement of the vital breath, there arises the specific distinction of time.
The procedure for worship is according to that specific time.

In all the Yoginītantras, there is the movement of the female messengers (dūtīs). By virtue of this movement, one should understand everywhere that there are the authorities of enjoyment and absorption, as well as sovereignty.

(35) Chapter VIII: The Movement of Yoginīs in the Gaṇacakra; The Movement within the Jñānacakra. First Day. Now, the movement from place to place of the Kulikā and the female messengers (*dūtī*) in the gaṇacakra is described.
Here, on the first day, at midnight, when the eastern face rises, there is the movement of Vajravārāhī as Kulikā from her position as the presiding deity in the center to the eastern petal.
