He who was a householder, an enjoyer of small huts, a servant, a plowman, and a merchant—
a fool who sold the True Dharma— was not made a leader of the community.
Thus, the Vajrācārya who bears the banner of omniscience should be placed facing east by the patron during the *vīrabhojya* feast.
To his right, a row of monks and Vajradhara Ācāryas—arranged in order from the eldest to the youngest—should be seated facing east.
Then, according to their seniority, a row of novice Ācāryas (*cellaka*) should be seated facing north, beginning from the southwest (*nairṛtya*) and extending as far as the southeast (*agni*).

Starting from Īśāna and ending with Vāyu, the row of householders and *ācāryas* should be arranged facing south, distinguished by seniority (*jyeṣṭha*) and juniority (*kaniṣṭha*). Having begun with the Lord of the Gaṇas (*Gaṇādhipa*), the row of mendicants (*bhikṣu*) and *ācāryas* should be formed starting from the north-west (*vāyavya*) and ending with the south-west (*nairṛtya*). Food, drink, and other offerings should be placed in the east. In the center, in the absence of a dust-mandala (*rajomaṇḍala*), a square area should be prepared with cow-dung water; having performed worship there with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, [one should place the offerings] on the left side of the Lord of the Gaṇas.

One should establish a single action-seal (*karmamudrā*) by assuming the seal of the Lord of the Assembly (*gaṇādhipamudrā*). Otherwise, drinking without a *yoginī* is not prescribed even in the Hero’s Feast (*vīrabhojya*).
Therefore, for the sake of increasing merit, the patron must necessarily offer a seal to the Lord of the Assembly.
However, where between a monk and a Vajradhara the elder is ignorant and the younger is the instructor, there the younger is the leader of the assembly (*gaṇādhipati*).
The elder, being ignorant, is to be satisfied in another house.
Likewise, in another tantra, it is stated that even yoginīs who have received initiation are to be worshipped separately in another house during the *vīrabhojya* feast.
First, the bhikṣuṇīs are consecrated facing east, distinguished by seniority and juniority; the cellikyas are consecrated facing north; and the upāsikās are consecrated facing south.
To the left of the leader of the assembly, the preceptor must be positioned by the patron.
Otherwise, without the proper means (*upāya*), the consumption of meat by the Lord of the Gaṇa (*gaṇādhipati*) is not prescribed in the *vīrabhojya* feast.
Therefore, the patron (*dānapati*) must necessarily provide the means for the Lord of the Gaṇa.
The remaining mandalas and so forth are as before; in the center are the food and drink, and so forth, as previously described.
Then, by circling counter-clockwise starting from the leader of the gaṇas, the solid foods and soft foods should be offered.
The drink should be given in a shallow bowl or a coconut shell and the like.

Then, having purified, awakened, ignited, and transformed the liquor and other substances into nectar, and having presented the offering cakes and so forth, one should sprinkle them with the previously mentioned pill.
Then, one should purify with the syllable *oṃ* using the left hand, and awaken with the syllable *āḥ* using the right hand.
Covering it with the *añjali* gesture, one should ignite it with the syllable *hūṃ*.

Having rendered it nectar with the syllable *hoḥ* by means of the *garuḍamudrā*, one should draw a triangle—the *dharmodaya*—on the ground with the tip of the left ring finger using a drop of liquor, and a circle as a drop in its center.

In its center is the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*), consisting of thirty-seven deities, transparent and like a magical reflection (*pratisenā*); one should perform its propitiation according to the procedure to be described.
[One should perform it] with the syllables equal to the name of the field-protectors (*kṣetrapāla*) and so forth, and the city or village, using the vowels *a* and *ā*.
A name consisting of two syllables is formed by the first and last syllables [of the verse].
A three-syllable name occurs when the name is formed by the first, middle, and final syllables among those of unequal number.
Oṃ at the beginning, the name in the middle, and Āḥ Hūṃ at the end;
for example: Oṃ [Name] Āḥ Hūṃ.
Bali! Grasp, grasp! Make the minds of all sentient beings peaceful, peaceful! Svāhā! Likewise: (Oṃ) Hārītī, accept this food offering, kṣīṃ! Svāhā!
Two balls of food for Hārītī:
Oṃ dūtike agragrāsaṃ pratīccha svāhā, oṃ āṃ hūṃ.
Having consecrated them with this mantra, one should place them on the ground until the end of the meal.
Oṃ khakhakhāhi khāhi, ucchiṣṭabali, ucchiṣṭabhakṣaka svāhā! This is the mantra for the *ucchiṣṭabali*.
At the appropriate time, everything should be performed individually.
Thereafter, food and drink should be partaken of by all the preceptors together with their disciples.
When someone engages in dispute or quarrel, he should be expelled.
However, if a monk or a householder displays pride, one should then inquire about his spiritual power (*sāmarthya*).
If he demonstrates powers such as the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) and so forth, then he shall be the leader of the community for everyone in all matters.
Otherwise, due to pride in one's learning or pride in being the eldest among those who have received initiation, a monk or a householder does not become a leader of the community (*gaṇanāyaka*).
Whoever was previously a monk is the leader of the community everywhere.
Now, if one who has been excluded from the feast of heroes (*vīrabhojya*) requests punishment, then the leader of the community must grant him punishment regarding food, drink, and so forth.
In this manner, this procedure must be performed everywhere by the patron (dānapati) in the circle of the assembly and at the feast for heroes.

(63) Chapter XII: The Practice of Mantras. Now the procedure for the accomplishment of mantras is being stated. Here, the verses to be recited below are taught for the purpose of drawing the mandala and for the accomplishment of mudrās and mantras. They are as follows:
In mountain caves and groves, on the shores of the great ocean,
and in primordial siddhi-cemeteries— there one should draw the maṇḍala.
Thus, the Blessed One has taught this instruction on the locations for the purpose of accomplishing the expansion of activities and mundane attainments (*laukikasiddhi*).
Having constructed the mandala to be described in those aforementioned locations, one should accomplish immobilization (*stambhana*), delusion (*mohana*), and pinning down (*kīlana*) upon a mountain.
Having constructed the mandala in a ravine thick with trees, one should accomplish subjugation (*vaśya*) and summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*).
Having drawn a maṇḍala on the bank of a clear pond in a grove, the practitioner should accomplish pacifying (śāntika) and enriching (pauṣṭika) rites.
Having drawn a maṇḍala on the shore of the great ocean, he should accomplish rites of causing hatred (vidveṣa), expulsion (ucchāṭana), and killing (māraṇa).
Having drawn a maṇḍala in a cremation ground, the mantra-practitioner should accomplish the extraction of the ḍākinī-mantra, which is the primordial accomplishment (ādisiddhi).
Likewise, there are mundane accomplishments (*laukika-siddhi*).
Here, one should accomplish the accomplishment of treasure (*nidhāna-siddhi*) on the mountain;
one should accomplish the accomplishment of jewels (*ratna-siddhi*) in the cave.
One should accomplish the siddhi of *rasa* in a bower;
one should accomplish the siddhi of the sword on the shore of the great ocean;
one should accomplish the siddhi of collyrium in a cremation ground.
The mantra-practitioner should also accomplish [the goal] according to the procedure taught in the Tantra.

Here, first of all, having drawn the mandala in a cremation ground and performed a great worship, on the full moon day of Caitra in the first year, one should offer the *argha* with the root mantra and recite the root mantra using a rosary made of human teeth.

Every month, on each full moon day beginning with the fifth, one should perform a fire offering (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth of three hundred thousand [recitations], using the substances prescribed in the *Karmaprasara*.
Thus, in one year, one should recite thirty-six hundred thousand times and perform a fire offering of three hundred and sixty thousand times.
The root mantra is: *oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru kaṃ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasaṃvaraṃ svāhā*.
Then, in the second year, according to that same procedure, one should recite the heart-mantra for one year and perform fire offerings:
*oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hreṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus is the six-syllable heart mantra.
By that same procedure, in the third year, one should recite and offer oblations with the near-heart mantra:
Oṃ hrīḥ haḥ haḥ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus is the seven-syllable subsidiary heart mantra (*upahṛdayamantra*).
Then, by that same procedure, in the fourth year, one should recite and offer oblations with the armor mantra (*kavacamantra*):
*oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hiṃ haṃ huṃ phaṭ*.
Thus ends the eight-syllable armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*).
Then, in the fifth year, by that same procedure, one should recite and perform fire offerings (*homa*) with the heart mantra of Vajravārāhī:
*oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā*.
Thus, through the purity of the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*), one recites the ten-syllable heart-mantra.
Then, in the sixth year, by that same procedure, one should recite and perform fire-offerings (*homa*) with the goddess’s armor-mantra (*devīkavacamanttra*):
*oṃ vaṃ yoṃ moṃ hrīṃ hreṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus ends the eight-syllable Great Armor Mantra (*mahākavacamantra*).
In this manner, for the six mantras, the recitation (*japa*) of two hundred and sixteen million [times] over six years must be performed;
furthermore, twenty-one hundred and sixty thousand fire offerings (*homa*) must be made, whereby the purification of the body of the yogins occurs.
Now, for the sake of the purification of the four faces, the recitation of the mantra of the four faces is described. Here,

at the time of the sun’s transit into Capricorn (makara-saṃkrānti), having drawn a maṇḍala on the shore of the great ocean and having offered the *argha* to the Ḍākinī, one should perform three hundred thousand recitations each month, with a fire offering (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth of that amount, on each full moon day,
for the mantra of the eastern face accompanied by the name of Vajraḍākinī and ending in *huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha vajraḍākinī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the fourteen-syllable mantra for the eastern face. One should recite nine hundred thousand [times] over three months and perform ninety thousand fire offerings (*homa*) using a rosary as prescribed in the *Karmaprasara-sādhana*—using a human bone rosary in the first month, a camel bone rosary in the second, and [an elephant bone rosary] in the third.
One should recite [the mantra] with a cord made of camel-hair and perform fire offerings (*homa*) with the substances prescribed in the *Karmaprasara*.

Then, during the transition of the sun into Aries (*meṣasaṃkrānti*), having drawn a maṇḍala in a secluded place and offered the water of respect (*argha*) to Lāmā, one should recite the mantra of the right face three hundred thousand times each month and perform the fire offering with a tenth part of that amount.
For each completion:
in the first month, with a rosary of lotus seeds; in the second, with a rosary of seeds from red sandalwood; in the third, with a rosary of red guñjā berries.
In this manner, nine hundred thousand recitations and nine thousand fire-oblations (homa) should be performed.
Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa vajralāme hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
This twelve-syllable mantra of the right face should be recited nine hundred thousand times, and one should perform nine thousand fire offerings (homa).
Then, during the solar transit into Cancer, having drawn a maṇḍala on a mountain and offered the water of honor (argha) to Khaṇḍarohā, [this should be done] every month.
One should recite the mantra of the western face three hundred thousand times and perform a fire offering (*homa*) with a tenth part of that amount.

In the first month, one should recite using a rosary of *putrajīva* beads; in the second, using a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads; and in the third, using a rosary of *riṣṭika* beads. The practitioner of the mantra should perform the fire offering with the substances prescribed in the *Karmaprasara*. Thus: Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya Vajrakhaṇḍarohā hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Thus, one should recite the eighteen-syllable mantra of the western face nine hundred thousand times and perform nine ten-thousand-fold fire offerings (*homa*).

Then, at the transit of the sun into Libra (*tulā-saṃkrānti*), having drawn a mandala in a bower and offered the *argha* oblation to Rūpiṇī, one should recite the mantra of the northern face three hundred thousand times each month and perform thirty thousand fire offerings with the substances for the expansion of ritual activities (*karmaprasara-dravya*).

In the first month, one should recite with a crystal rosary; in the second, with a rosary of pearl beads; in the third, with a rosary of conch-shell beads. Thus, over the course of three months, one should recite nine hundred thousand times and perform ten thousand fire offerings (*homa*).
One should recite and perform fire offerings with the eighteen-syllable mantra of the northern face: *oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vajra-vajrarūpiṇi huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus, in one year, one should recite thirty-six lakhs; one should perform thirty lakhs and sixty thousand fire-oblations (homa), after which the purification of the mouth occurs.
Now, the recitation of the mantra for the purpose of purifying the eight doors, beginning with the mouth and ears, is described.

Here, in the second year, at the transit of the sun into Capricorn (*makara-saṃkrānti*), having drawn a mandala on the shore of the great ocean and having offered the water-offering (*argha*) to Kākāsyā, one should perform the recitation using a rosary of human teeth:
during the first fortnight, for fifteen days, one should recite the eight-line [mantra] fifteen times; during the second fortnight, [one should recite it] twenty-eight times.
With the third [beads], an akṣasūtra made of wild boar tusks;

thus, for one and a half months, one should recite four hundred thousand [mantras] and perform four thousand five hundred fire offerings (*homayet*) with the substances mentioned in the section on the ritual activities of the eastern face.
Oṃ namo bhagavate vīreśāya vajrakākāsye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the first quarter, consisting of nineteen syllables.

Then, having drawn a maṇḍala in a secluded corner of the sacrificial pit and having offered the *argha* oblation to Ulūkāsyā, one should perform the recitation of the mantra four hundred thousand times over a period of three fortnights, using the rosary described for Lāmā.
The fire offering (*homa*) is performed with one-tenth [of the total number].
*Oṃ mahākalpāgnisaṃnibhāya vajrolūkāsye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. This is the eighteen-syllable mantra of the second line.

Then, at the solar transit of Aries, having drawn the mandala on the mountain and having offered the *argha* to Śvānāsyā, one should recite [the mantra] for four hundred and fifty thousand times over the course of a month and a half according to the procedure taught for the *khaṇḍarohā* rosary;
one should perform the fire offering (*homa*) with a tenth part of that amount.
Oṃ jaṭāmakuṭotkaṭāya vajraśvānāsye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Thus is the mantra of the third line, consisting of seventeen syllables.

Then, having drawn a maṇḍala in a bower during the half-day of the bull [nakṣatra], and having offered the *argha* to Śūkarāsyā, one should recite [the mantra] four hundred thousand times together with Rūpiṇī for a month and a half according to the procedure prescribed for the rosary;
and one should perform forty-five thousand *homa* offerings.
Oṃ daṃṣṭrākākarālograbhīṣaṇamukhāya vajrasūkarāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the twenty-two-syllable mantra of the fourth line.

Then, at the rising of Cancer, having drawn a maṇḍala in a lotus pond like a bower, and having offered the *argha* to Yamadāḍhī, one should recite four hundred thousand [mantras] along with half a month, according to the procedure for the rosary described by Rūpiṇī.
One should recite [the mantra] ten times its length and perform fire offerings (homa) one-tenth that amount.
*Oṃ sahasrabhujabhāsurāya vajrayamadāḍhi huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
This is the nineteen-syllable mantra of the fifth section.

Then, on Mount Siṃhārdhadina, having drawn a maṇḍala and offered the *argha* to Yamadūtī, one should recite [the mantra] for three fortnights—four hundred thousand and fifty thousand times—according to the procedure for the rosary taught by Khaṇḍarohā.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with a tenth part of that number, one should dismiss her with:
*oṃ paraśupāśodyataśūlakhaṭvāṅgadhāriṇe vajrayamadūti huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus, with twenty-five syllables, is the mantra of the sixth step.

Then, at the time of the transition of the sun into Libra (tulā-saṃkrānti), having drawn a maṇḍala in a garden and offered the *argha* oblation to Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, one should recite four hundred thousand and a half (*sārdha-catur-lakṣa*) mantras over the course of one and a half months, according to the sequence of the rosary beads described for Lāmā;
and one should perform forty-two thousand (*sārdha-catur-yuta*) fire offerings (*homa*).
Oṃ, to the one wearing a tiger-skin garment, O you with adamantine fangs, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Thus is the twenty-syllable mantra of the seventh step.

Then, at midday during the scorpion season, having drawn a maṇḍala on the shore of the ocean—or in the absence of an ocean, having drawn a maṇḍala on the bank of a salt-water pond—one should [perform the rite] with Yamamathanī. (67)

Having offered the *argha* water, one should recite the mantra for three fortnights according to the procedure for the rosary taught by Vajraḍākinī—namely, four hundred thousand and fifty thousand times. On each full moon day, one should perform fire offerings (*homa*) until they amount to forty-five thousand.
Oṃ mahādhūmāndhakāravapuṣāya vajrayamamathani hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Thus is the twenty-two-syllable mantra of the eighth step.
In this manner, one should recite it thirty-six hundred thousand times over the course of one year and perform thirty-six million fire offerings (*homa*).
Thereupon, purification of the channels of the mouth, anus, nose, ears, and eyes occurs.
Now, the recitation of the mantras for the twenty-four secondary members (*pratyaṅga*) is described.

Here, on the shore of the ocean—or if that is unavailable, on the shore of a salt-water pond—one should draw a mandala. On the new moon day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having offered the *argha* oblation to Pracaṇḍā, one should perform fifty thousand recitations over five lunar days and perform five thousand fire-offerings (*homa*).

Thus, having performed the mantra recitation of one hundred and fifty thousand times over fifteen days, and having performed the fire offering (*homa*) of fifteen thousand times, there is a mantra recitation of fifty thousand times for each individual rosary as prescribed by the Vajraḍākinīs. *Oṃ kara kara vajrapracaṇḍe vajrakaṇḍakapālin hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.* This twenty-syllable mantra is the first mantra for each limb.

Then, on the full moon day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having constructed a maṇḍala in a cave, a garden, or a forest, and having offered the *argha* oblation to Caṇḍākṣī, one should recite [the mantra] for one hundred and fifty thousand times over the course of a fortnight using the rosaries mentioned for Lāmā according to the previously described procedure, and perform fifteen thousand *homa* offerings with the mantra:
*oṃ kuru kuru vajracaṇḍākṣi vajrāmahākakāla hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus ends the twenty-syllable mantra of the second line.

Then, on the new moon day of the month of Pauṣa, having drawn a maṇḍala on a mountain and offered the *argha* oblation to Prabhāvatī, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and fifty thousand times over fifteen lunar days using the rosaries described by Khaṇḍarohā; one should perform ten thousand five hundred burnt offerings (*homa*).
Oṃ bandha bandha vajraprabhāvati vajrakakāla huṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the third line, consisting of nineteen syllables.

Then, on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, having drawn a maṇḍala in a grove or on the bank of a lotus pond, one should offer an *argha* oblation to Mahānasā and recite [the mantra] for fifteen days, totaling one hundred and fifty thousand times, using rosaries of beads made of *rūpīṇī*.
One should recite [the mantra] eleven thousand five hundred times and perform the fire offering (*homayet*).
*Oṃ trāsaya trāsaya vajramahānāse vajravikaṭadaṃṣṭrin hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
This is the twenty-three-syllable mantra of the fourth line.
Then, on the new moon day of the month of Māgha,

having drawn a maṇḍala in a bower or on the bank of a lotus pond, and having offered the *argha* oblation to Vīramatī, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and fifty thousand times with rosaries made of *rūpīṇī* seeds over the course of a fortnight, and perform ten thousand five hundred *homa* offerings with the mantra:
*oṃ kṣobhaya kṣobhaya vajravīramati vajrasurāvairin hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus, with twenty-two syllables, is the fifth *padamantra*.

Then, on the full moon day of the month of Māgha, having drawn a mandala on a mountain and having offered an *argha* to Kharvarī, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and fifty thousand times and perform eleven thousand five hundred fire offerings (*homa*) using rosaries made of the materials mentioned for Khaṇḍarohā over a period of fifteen nights.
Oṃ hrauṃ hrauṃ vajrakharvari vajrāmitābha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the sixteen-syllable mantra of the sixth step.

Then, on the new moon day of the month of Phālguna, having drawn a maṇḍala in a cave or a garden and having offered the water of honor (argha) to Laṅkeśvarī, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and fifty thousand times over a period of fifteen days using the rosaries mentioned for Lāmā.
One should perform eleven thousand five hundred *homa* offerings with the following sixteen-syllable mantra of the seventh line: *Oṃ hraḥ hraḥ Vajralakeśvari vajraprabha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, on the full moon day of Phālguna, having prepared a maṇḍala on the shore of the ocean or on the bank of a salt-water pond, one should offer an *argha* to the shade of a tree and recite the mantra five hundred and three times for fifteen days using rosaries made of *ḍākinī*-specified seeds; one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and fifty thousand times and perform ten thousand and five hundred fire offerings (*homa*).
Oṃ pheṃ pheṃ Vajradrumacchāye Vajradeha huṃ hūṃ phaṭ!

Thus is the sixteen-syllable mantra of the eighth line. Having offered the *argha* to Airāvatī according to the procedure taught by Pracaṇḍā, one should recite the mantra and perform the fire oblation (*homa*) on the new moon day of Caitra.

"Oṃ daha daha vajrairāvati vajrāṅkuśike hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ"—this is the eighteen-syllable mantra of the ninth line. And on the full moon day of Caitra, [one should worship] Mahābhairavā according to the procedure taught by Caṇḍākṣī.
Having offered the *argha* water, one should recite the mantra and perform the fire offering (*homa*).
*Oṃ paca paca vajramahābhairave vajrajaṭila hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
This is the twenty-syllable mantra of the tenth line.

Then, on the new moon day of Vaiśākha, having offered the *argha* oblation to Vāyuvegā according to the procedure taught by Prabhāvatī, one should recite the mantra and perform the fire offering (*homa*).
*Oṃ bhakṣa bhakṣa vajravāyuvege vajramahāvīra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ.* This is the eleven-pada mantra consisting of twenty syllables.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, according to the ritual prescribed by Mahānāsa, one should offer an *argha* oblation to Surābhakṣī and recite the mantra while performing fire offerings (*homa*).
Oṃ vasarudhirāntramālābalaṃ vine gṛhṇa gṛhṇa vajrasurābhakṣi vajrahūṃkāra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Thus [ends] the thirty-first [chapter]. (69)
The twelve-syllable mantra of the twelfth limb is as follows: *oṃ saptapātālagataṃ bhujagasarpaṃ vā tarjaya tarjaya vajraśyāmādevi vajrasubhadra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, on the new moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having offered the *argha* to the goddess Śyāmā according to the procedure taught by Vīramatī, one should recite the mantra and perform the fire offering (*homa*).
*Oṃ saptapātālagataṃ bhujagasarpaṃ vā tarjaya tarjaya vajraśyāmādevi vajrasubhadra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus is the thirteen-word mantra consisting of thirty-four syllables.
On the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having offered the *argha* to Subhadrā according to the ritual prescribed for Kharvarī, one should recite and perform homa with:
*oṃ ākaṭṭa ākaṭṭa vajrasubhadre vajrabhadra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus ends the fourteen-word mantra consisting of nineteen syllables.

Then, on the new moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, having offered the *argha* oblation to Hayakarṇā according to the procedure prescribed by Laṅkeśvarī, one should recite the mantra and perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ vajrahayakarṇe vajramahābhairava hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus ends the fifteen-syllable mantra of the fifteenth foot, consisting of nineteen syllables.

On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, having offered the *argha* oblation to Khagānanā according to the procedure described for Drumacchāyā, one should recite the mantra and perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
Oṃ jñauṃ jñauṃ vajrakhagānane vajravirūpākṣa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus is the sixteen-syllable mantra of the sixteenth [chapter].

Then, on the new moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, having offered the *argha* to Cakravegā according to the procedure taught for Pracaṇḍā, one should recite the mantra and perform the fire offering (*homa*).
Oṃ kṣmāṃ kṣmāṃ vajracakravege vajramahābala huṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the seventeen-syllable mantra of the seventeenth foot.
Then, on the full moon day, having offered the *argha* to Khaṇḍarohā according to the procedure taught by Caṇḍākṣī, one should recite the mantra and perform the fire offering (*homa*).
"Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ Vajrakhaṇḍarohe Vajraratnavajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the eighteen-syllable [mantra]. (18th)
This is the *padamantra*.

Then, on the new moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, having offered the *argha* to Śauṇḍinī according to the procedure taught by Prabhāvatī, one should recite the mantra and perform the fire offering (*homa*).
Oṃ hīṃ hīṃ Vajraśauṇḍini Vajrahayagrīva huṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus is the nineteen-syllable mantra consisting of seventeen syllables.
Then, on the full moon day, having offered the *argha* to Cakravarmiṇī according to the procedure taught by Mahānāsa, one should recite the mantra and perform fire offerings (*homa*).
Oṃ huṃ hūṃ vajracakra varmiṇi vajrākāśagarbha huṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus is the twenty-syllable mantra consisting of twenty parts.

Then, on the new moon day of the month of Āśvina, having offered the *argha* oblation to Suvīrā according to the procedure described by Vīramatī, one should recite the mantra and perform the fire offering (*homa*).
Oṃ kili kili vajrasuvīre vajraheruka hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus is the twenty-one-word mantra consisting of eighteen syllables.

Then, on the full moon day, having offered the *argha* oblation to Mahābalā according to the ritual prescribed for the *kharva* [day], one should recite the mantra and perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
Oṃ śili śili (70) vajramahābale vajrapadmanarteśvara hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the twenty-two-syllable mantra of the twenty-second foot.

Then, on the new moon day of the month of Kārttika, having offered the *argha* to the Universal Monarch (Cakravartinī) according to the procedure taught by the Queen of Laṅkā, one should recite the mantra and perform the fire offering (*homa*).
Oṃ hili hili vajracakravartini vajra vairocana huṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This twenty-three-syllable mantra consists of twenty-three words.

Then, on the full moon day, having constructed a maṇḍala according to the procedure described for Drumacchāyā, having offered the *argha* to Mahāvīryā, and having performed three hundred and fifty thousand recitations (*japa*) over fifteen days, one should perform ten thousand five hundred fire offerings (*homa*) with this mantra:
*oṃ dhili dhili vajramahāvīrye vajrasattva huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus, the mantra consists of eighteen syllables and twenty-four words.

In this manner, during the third year, one should recite the twenty-four-word mantra thirty-six hundred thousand times (*ṣaṭtriṃśallakṣam*) and perform thirty-six hundred thousand oblations (*ṣaṭtriṃśadayutāni*).
In this way, over the course of three years, there are ten million plus eight hundred thousand recitations and one million plus eight hundred thousand oblations.
Thereupon, the purification of each individual limb occurs for the yogins.
This is the procedure for the recitation of the mantra.

Alternatively, the twenty-four-syllable mantra should be recited and offered as oblation according to the aforementioned method, by means of the twenty-four fortnights corresponding to the twenty-four transits (*saṃkrānti*).
During the transit of Scorpio, on the half-day of Scorpio—

and likewise when the Sun has traversed the half of the ascendant in each of the twelve signs— one should draw the mandala, offer the argha, and recite the respective mantras and perform homa for as long as it takes to prepare the gaṇacakra, until the deity's injunction is fulfilled.
One should recite the twenty-four-word mantra for as long as twelve years.

In all cases, the syllable *oṃ* precedes each word of the mantra. Then, for each individual limb, one should place *vajra-* at the beginning of the name of the messenger (*dūtī*) and the name of the hero (*vīra*). Wherever the name does not already begin with *vajra-*, one should append *hrasva-dīrgha-hūṃ-hūṃ* at its end, followed by the syllable *phaṭ*.
One [syllable].
Where there are three *hūṃ* syllables at the end, there all [syllables] are long, and there are two *phaṭ* syllables; this is the rule for reciting mantras everywhere.

Here, all mantras, beginning with the root mantras and so forth, should have *svāhā* at their end when invoking the deity, in place of the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, according to each respective ritual action.
Likewise, when offering the *argha* water, during worship, and during the recitation of mantras for pacification (*śānti*), they end with *namaḥ*;
during the recitation for nourishment (*puṣṭi*), they end with *svāhā*;
and during the recitation for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), they end with *vauṣaṭ*.
In the recitation for subjugation (*vaśya*), the mantras end with *vaṣaṭ*.
In the ritual procedures for the actions described for the left and right faces, as well as those described for the front and back faces, all [mantras] should be made to end with *huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

In the sequence of the fire offering (*homa*), all mantras should end with *svāhā*. However, during the ritual procedures prescribed for the left and right faces, as well as those prescribed for the front and back faces, when performing the fire offering again, all mantras must individually end with *hūṃ phaṭ*.

Through the recitation and fire offering of inverted mantras, by drawing the mandala in an inverted location, by using an inverted fire pit (*kuṇḍa*), and by means of inverted fire-offering substances, the entire accomplishment of siddhi becomes fruitless.
[This is] for those of immature intellect.

Therefore, having drawn the mandala to be described, having offered the *argha* to the deities of the mantras, and having performed the recitation of the mantras, one should accomplish the mantra for up to twelve years by means of the sacrificial substances to be described, using the fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) that will be described.
This continues until there is a restriction regarding the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) for the performance of the *gaṇacakra*.

Then, having performed the *gaṇacakra* for three fortnights, on the full moon day, by the power of the deity, the practitioner becomes the leader of the assembly (*gaṇanāyaka*) and attains accomplishment together with the *gaṇacakra* through this procedure.

By another procedure, having accomplished a single mantra over twelve years and having taken hold of a single action-seal (*karmamudrā*) according to the restriction of the deity, one attains accomplishment.
He does not become a vessel for any worldly accomplishments whatsoever; because of his lack of vigor (*hīnavīryatva*), he becomes a servant to all the accomplishments achieved in the *gaṇacakra*.

Thus, at the specific time of accomplishing all worldly siddhis, the yogin should perform [the practice] after having worshipped the female messengers (*dūtī*) and the innate accomplished ones (*sahaja-siddha*) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Thus is the rule of the Blessed Heruka in the *Lakṣābhidhāna*.

Thus has the ritual procedure for the worship of the thirty-six female messengers (*dūtī*) been taught by me, the illustrious Vajrapāṇi, according to specific times, through this commentary and the rule of the Lord of Heroes, for the sake of accomplishing all siddhis for those who possess thorough knowledge of the means (*upāya*).
This is the rule for the ritual procedure for the worship of the female messengers.

(72) Chapter XIII: The Threefold Siddhi of the Messenger (Dūtikā). Commentary on CS 7AB: Now, those who bestow the inferior, middling, and superior siddhis are described by the words beginning with "the messenger" (dūtikā). Here, the messengers are the three types of innate ones (sahajā), such as Mahāvīryā and the rest.
The heroes (vīra) are the accomplished ones (siddha), such as the twenty-four Vajrasattvas and the rest.
Among them, eight are inferior, dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), because they bestow the siddhis of the netherworld;
likewise, eight are middling, dwelling on earth, because they bestow siddhis such as sovereignty;
and eight are superior, moving through the sky (khecaras), because they bestow the siddhis of the desire realm (kāmāvacara).
The four ḍākinīs are also superior because they bestow the accomplishments (siddhi) of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
Kākāsyā and the others are inferior because they bestow the accomplishments of the hungry ghosts and animals.
Thus, whatever is accomplished by the yogin through worldly truth (*laukikasatya*), all that fruit of accomplishment is threefold: inferior, middling, and superior.
Therefore, what is the use of that which is accomplished by them, since it does not result in Buddhahood—the cause for the exhaustion of birth, old age, and death—for yogins?
Having understood this, yogins seeking liberation should cultivate the accomplishment of desire with a mind turned inward.
Such is the rule of the Tathāgata.

(73) Chapter XIV: The Meditation upon the Perfection of Love and the Initiations. Commentary on CS 7cd. Now, the meditation on *mahāmudrā* is explained by the passage beginning with "with the mind internalized" (*antargatena manasā*). Here, in the Mantra Vehicle (*mantranaya*), within the *prajñopāya* tantras, this *vajrapada* is to be understood through the terminology of intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*) across various tantras and different tantra systems. The phrase "with the mind internalized" (*antargatena manasā*) has its preceding words and so forth [as follows].
This vajra-word was also spoken by the Blessed Buddha in the *Śrī-samāja* in twenty-five thousand verses: “From the vajra-paryaṅka posture, one should gaze at the mind within the jewel;
until it attains stainlessness, filled with the bliss of the outflow and so forth.”
Likewise:
Having established the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, one should not emit the *bodhicitta*;
rather, one should meditate upon the image of the Buddha as the entirety of the triple world without exception.
Thus, here the condensed meaning of this vajra-word is to be understood through these two verses;
it is stated in this tantra by means of a half-verse.
Here, the *bodhicitta* contained within the *vajramaṇi* is called the "internal mind" (*antargatamanas*).

With that internal mind—the *bodhicitta* which has not fallen—one should meditate upon the image of the Buddha characterized by the three realms, whether in connection with a *karmamudrā* or a *jñānamudrā*.

The yogin should meditate, in its entirety, upon the three realms—characterized by desire, form, and formlessness, consisting of the nature of all stable and moving entities, and endowed with the excellence of all aspects.

That very Perfection of Wisdom, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, is called "the accomplishment of desire" (*kāmasiddhi*) in this tantra by the Blessed One, because it is a wisdom-tantra (*prajñātantra*).
The yogi should meditate upon that accomplishment of desire.
Here, "desire" (*kāma*) is great passion (*mahārāga*), Vajrasattva, the Great Purpose, the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*).
"Accomplishment (*siddhi*) is Mahāmudrā, the Perfection of Wisdom endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
Alternatively, desire is non-referential great compassion, while accomplishment is referential great emptiness, because these are to be personally realized by yogins.
Thus, the latter accomplishment is superior to the accomplishments of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*).

"One should meditate upon that Mahāmudrā—the accomplishment of desire, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of the aspects of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*)—which bestows the qualities of a Buddha such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, for the sake of Buddhahood.
This is the rule of the Tathāgatas in those intermediate [tantras].
"In that regard, it is to be understood through another tantra," according to the word of the Tathāgata.
The cultivation of this very [reality] is twofold:
the cultivation of the prior image and the cultivation of the subsequent image.
The cultivation of the prior image consists of the cultivation of signs such as smoke and so forth, up to the limit of the image.
Once the image has been seen and the *liṅga* has been established within the *bhaga*, subsequent meditation is for the purpose of increasing the supreme, immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*).
Furthermore, having abandoned both the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*), one should meditate upon the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) for the increase of great bliss.
In this regard, the Blessed One stated in the twelve-thousand-verse *Paramādibuddha* that there is a prohibition against the meditation on the action-seal and the knowledge-seal.

And thus the Blessed One said: "Having abandoned the action-seal (karmamudrā) and the conceptualized wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā), one should meditate upon the great seal (mahāmudrā) through the yoga of the supreme unchanging."
Thus,
in the initial practice, there is the prior cultivation:
as long as the yogin does not relinquish the *bodhicitta*.
In the womb, one attains that uninterrupted, supreme bliss for as long as [the period lasts].
One should constantly meditate upon oneself as the image of the Buddha, endowed with that very form of bliss, until the semen becomes stable.
Thus, this vajra-word should also be understood in the sense of consecration (*sekārtha*).

Here, in this king of tantras consisting of wisdom and means, the Blessed One indeed stated that for the sake of the practice of the ignorant, the bliss born of the two organs— which arises through passion for the action-seal (*karmamudrā*)— is called "wisdom-knowledge" (*prajñājñāna*).
By way of worldly truth;
not by way of ultimate truth. Why?
"The fourth is that again, likewise," according to the words of the Blessed One.
In this context, those of immature intellect will say that the very same third, the gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), is the fourth consecration.
To that it is said:

In this context, if the third is the gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), and that very same third is designated by the word "suchness" (*tathatā*) as the fourth, then there would be the fault of redundancy, as it would be a restatement of what has already been expressed.
Alternatively, it might be the speech of the ignorant:
the cause is the third and the fruit is the fourth.
Because there is no difference between cause and fruit, the fourth [moment] is also established as the third;
therefore it is said:
"This is not indeed the Blessed One’s... (75)
The aforementioned [teaching] is from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
Why?
Because the Blessed One has taught the three mudrās for the sake of accomplishing the three fruits.
In this Mantra system, there are three kinds of fruits, distinguished as the accomplishments (siddhi) of desire-form and omniscience.
Among these, the accomplishment of the action-seal (karmamudrā) is the fruit of the desire realm;
the accomplishment of the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā) is the fruit of the form realm.

(80) Chapter XV: The Worship of the Great Secret; A Commentary on CS 8ab. Now, the worship of the great secret is explained beginning with the words "by one's own [fluid]" (*svareta*).
Here, in other tantras concerning wisdom and means, worship is twofold: external worship and internal worship.

Among these, external worship consists of the satiation of the aggregates, elements, and so forth, by means of the five services (*pañcopacāra*) and so on, as well as the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*).

Internal worship consists of the four drops of one’s own semen that have not been emitted, located in the secret place, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the forehead; these possess the natures of outflow (*niḥsyanda*), maturation (*vipāka*), human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and purity (*vaimalya*).

By means of them—through their distinct characteristics and dissimilarities from the various [stages of] maturation, crushing, and the absence of marks—one worships the Buddhas as the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and the Bodhisattvas as the elements of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties.

By the word "and" (ca), one should worship the elements such as earth and the elements of objects such as form with the drops that do not fall from the mind of awakening—that is, with the moments of great immutable bliss; this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Furthermore, externally, one should worship with fallen drops that have been tasted, for the sake of external purification.

Internal worship, for the sake of attaining the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), is performed with the drops of one's own semen situated within the jewel; such is the rule for the ritual of worship with drops.
(81) Chapter XVI: Liberation from All Sins. Commentary on CS 8cd–9ab: Now, liberation from all sins is described by means of the verse beginning with *darśana*.
Here, vision (*darśana*) is twofold: external and internal;
likewise for touch (*sparśana*).
Here, there is the vision of the external consort (*karmamudrā*), the conceptualization of the wisdom consort (*jñānamudrā*),
and the touching of their faces, breasts, and vulvas.
It is by means of these two— vision and touch— that [the result is attained].

Likewise, within oneself, there is the vision of the images of all Buddhas of the three realms without exception, which is the vision of Mahāmudrā; and by those two, namely vision and touch, there is the experience of great bliss.
Likewise, it occurs through hearing and recollection as well.

In this context, through hearing the true Dharma and through the recollection of the Guru, the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, the Vīras, and the Vīreśvarīs—by means of these two, namely hearing and recollection—one is liberated from all sins. That is to say, one is liberated from all those [sins] committed by body, speech, and mind, such as the five acts of immediate retribution and the ten unwholesome paths of action. Having been granted permission, one remains established in the restraint (*saṃvara*) of not committing further sins.
Furthermore, even if permitted, one is not liberated from the misdeeds committed through greed and so forth in any circumstance;
thus, there is no doubt.

In this manner, according to the sequence described, the yogi who is free from the fourteen root downfalls [attains] through the cultivation of great bliss by means of the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*, with the bodhicitta that does not fall away.
